On motion of Sir Robert Borden (Prime Minister) Bill No. 165, to consolidate and amend the Acts respecting the Ottawa Improvement Commission-the Minister of Finance-was read the second time, and the Houise went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 2-Annual grant authorized:

I notice in the press this morning that the city of Ottawa and the Government have not come to terms as regards their mutual relations. Will the Minister of Finance tell us what is the state of the negotiations and if there is any expectation of a fair settlement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My colleague the Minister of Public Works will be better able to make a statement on the matter.

A great many conferences have been held between the representatives of the city of Ottawa and the Government regarding the amount that should be paid Ottawa for services rendered by the city to the Government. I think it will be unnecessary, and probably it might be improper, for me to go into a long detailed recital of the whole transaction, because I find it exceedingly difficult 'to bring myself to the conclusion that the city is entitled

to anything. If it were not for the Government, Ottawa would be only a by-town with a few saw-mills; there would be no city of Ottawa. It might not be prudent for me to state exactly how I feel about the matter. In the outset, the city wanted between $600,000 and $700,000 from the Government for the services they say they have rendered. They talk about maintaining hospitals for the benefit of the Government-

They are needed.
Mr. CARVELL-and they want thousands of dollars for the maintenance of those hospitals. They even fight about the intersections at street corners, because where we pay our improvement taxes along the side of the street they say that there is a little square in the corner that we do not pay for. Indeed, there is nothing on earth that the human mind can conceive which they do not want. I am speaking pretty plainly, but it is time I spoke my mind. It practically amounts to this:	Every man and
every woman in Ottawa are drawing something directly out of the Dominion Treasury and now they want to draw something collectively. I have concurred in a proposed agreement the substance of which is contained in to-day's Order Paper in the resolution on page 9. That proposes that we will pay to Ottawa for the next ten years the sum of seventy-five thousand dollars annually for the services which they allege they are performing for the Government. I use the word "allege" advisedly, because I do not think there is anything to it at all. The whole $75,000 is a clean present from the people of Canada to the city of Ottawa.
A "greed' present.
No, a clean one.
A neat present.

Possibly. In addition
to that, we have agreed-and this, I admit, is business; in fact, it is my own suggestion and I think it is the proper method- to pay the city of Ottawa for the water service which we receive the same as any other person would pay for that service. I think the rate is a very generous one. We agree to Ray 13 cents per thousand gallons supplied, for the first 200,000,000 gallons, and 10 cents per thousand gallons for the water supplied over that amount in any one year. The price, I think, is extremely generous; yet, it is a service which the city of Ottawa is performing for the Government and for which we should
pay it. I am not disposed to split hairs about the amount but I think it is very generous.
Have they always been paid for that service?

No, we have been paying $15,000 a year and I think it has been put on the ground of fire protection. Yet the city of Ottawa is entitled to protect the buildings of the Government just as it would be the buildings of any one else; that is what you pay taxes for. We are under no obligation to pay them because they have a fire department which would go out in case of trouble; that is their business. But, the water service is .entirely on a different basis. I have always contended that the city of Ottawa has not been fairly treated in so far as the water service is concerned. We are using a great amount of water-a greater amount than I think we should use. If one of those employees out on the street wants to wet the street he would use as much water as would be required for twenty-fiye streets. But it has been on a flat rate and it did not make any difference how much was used. I think that the city of Ottawa has contributed to the Government more than it should have contributed in the way of water.
Does the city get the water by gravitation?

No, the city pumps it out of the Ottawa river. Then we propose that all buildings now leased by the Government shall pay the water tax the same as any other private party. In the past the moment the Government leased a building the water tax ceased. That is not fair to the city. They have what I have always considered the most terribly antiquated system of assessing water taxes in this city but it suits them and I suppose . it should suit us and as long as we have property in this city we could comply with the laws which they see fit to adopt. Instead of asking people to pay for the water they consume, they require them to pay on the basis of the taxation of the property. If a man has a vacant lot without any building on it and if he does not use a drop of water, he pays on the taxation of the property. If he has a little piece of land and a million dollar building upon it, he pays according to the taxation. It is a very antiquated system but if it suits Ottawa it suits me. If we rent a building from any person in Ottawa, the city is entitled to the water rates according



to the law whatever it may be and that is what we are providing for here.
When the Government rent a building what is the basis upon which it goes; is it on the basis of so much per square foot of space or so much per cubic foot?
I think the basis is that the landlord gets every cent that the traffic will bear. '
I have no doubt of that.

That has been my experience in the city of Ottawa. Now, to answer my hon. friend, we try to come down to a square foot basis in reference to the matter and. the rents run all the way from fifty cents up to $1.10 and $1.15 per square foot. But after all I do not know that I have been long enough at it to get at the bottom of it. There is a great deal of juggling going on in my judgment about leasing public buildings in Ottawa. If a man has a building in Ottawa that he wants to rent to the Government he will always find somebody who will recommend that the Government ought to rent it and he will always find some official to recommend that the rent be placed at a rate that is high. The Public Works Department has to get that down as far as they can and it is a see-saw until we come down to a final conclusion. I hope the time will come when the Dominion Government will own their own public buildings in Ottawa and I am sure it would be a good investment, if the Government can find the money, to erect public buildings in this city and get rid of some of the conditions which we have to face now.
In addition, we are carrying out an old agreement that has been in existence for many years regarding the maintenance of what is now called Connaught Place, formerly Dufferin and Sappers bridges, over the Rideau canal, the bridge over the Rideau canal at Laurier avenue and the maintenance of the sidewalks and streets on Wellington street. The agreement used to go from Connaught Place to Bank street; now that the Government have bought all the land westward to the Perley Home, so called, we are extending the contract to cover Wellington street as far west as the Perley Home.
All east of the Perley Home?

We have bought all the land on Wellington street and we are extending the agreement westward , to the

western boundary of the Perley Home. We also agree that we shall be subject to bylaws regarding local improvements. If it be the law that a property owner shall contribute the whole or a portion of the cost of a sidewalk or a street opposite his land, the Government agree to put themselves in the same position and will pay their full share of the taxation whatever it may be.
Finally, it is proposed that an Order in Council passed a great many years ago by which, for a certain consideration, the city of Ottawa did not tax the income of civil servants, shall be discontinued. I see no reason why the Civil Service should not be liable to the ordinary laws of the land the same as anybody else is. Therefore, I am doing all I can to put the city of Ottawa in the position where it can legally tax civil servants. If they do not want to do it, that is their business and not mine, but I do not feel like being a party to preventing the city of Ottawa from assessing the ordinary income tax upon civil servants according to the law whatever it may be.
That is very necessary in view of the fact that the Civil Service bids fair to be half the population of the ci*y of Ottawa.

Large or small, I am a great believer in taxation, and I do not believe in exemption from taxation. I have upheld that principle all my life and I would not be associated with an industry that would go to any municipality and ask for exemption from taxation. I have never done that in my life and I never will. If a business cannot pay its fair share of the municipal taxes, it had better go out of business, or if an individual cannot pay his share of the municipal taxes he had better leave and go some place else.

Will my hon. friend
apply that principle to Victory bonds?

Yes, I would. I am the only man in the House of Commons who is on record publicly up to within the last six months as opposing exemption of income from Victory bonds, if that ds any satisfaction to my hon. friend. I am afraid that some of my hon. friends did not agree with me in that but if my hon. friend will look up Hansard two years ago he will find what my views were then in reference to the exemption of Victory bonds.
Did they follow you on the other side?
No, they did not. My hon. friend from Maisonneuve was with me on that view-I will grant that.
Yes, I was.

If I have spoken with a great deal of frankness on this subject, I will say that I have intended to especially as the hon. member for Maisonneuve wanted my views upon the question. I do not know whether the city of Ottawa intends accepting the proposed agreement or not. I was notified yesterday that they had declined to do so but that they were willing to accept an agreement for five years. They thought the agreement was fair but they wanted a chance to come back again at the end of five years and get another bite. Not with my consent. That is all I have to say about it. If the city of Ottawa will sign the agreement I will ask Parliament to adopt this resolution and also pass a Bill simply confirming the resolution. That is the position in which the matter stands this morning.

What would be the
probable increase over the former allowance?

I will put it in this way. For the past ten years the Government has been giving $100,000 to the Ottawa Improvement Commission and paying $15,000 a year to the city of Ottawa for fire protection. The new arrangement proposes that $150,000 a year be given to the Improvement Commission, and the city will get $75,000 cash by way of a grant in payment for certain claimed services. The city also will get water rates on the basis of thirteen cents per thousand gallons, up to 250,000,000 gallons, and ten cents a gallon thereafter. It is pretty hard to form a correct opinion as to what the payment for this service will amount to. I have tried to estimate the amount, and my judgment is it will be about $25,000. That, however, is only an estimate, because they do not have meters in this city; they do not seem to know anything about it, and they cannot tell how much water would be consumed in an ordinary building. I have some knowledge of the matter from my business experience in other parts of Canada, a very considerable knowledge, in fact. I think the amount of water consumed in this case would be the same per thousand of population, and from my own business knowledge I put $25,000 as being practically the maximum which the city will receive. Then in addition to that
What is the cost per thousand gallons for pumping, exclusive of overhead charges?

I do not know; I cannot get from the city exactly what it is; but I would say that, exclusive of overhead charges, a couple of cents a thousand .gallons would be a very large charge. I am speaking now from my own business knowledge of conditions elsewhere in Canada- in fact, I know that the company with which I am connected is pumping water at a cent and-a-half per thousand gallons. That is exclusive of overhead charges, and we are not losing any money on it, either.
To finish the answer to the question of my hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx), I cannot tell exactly what the city will receive from water rates on the leased buildings, but my estimate is $7,500. That is only an estimate, and the charge made for the purpose will really depend upon how the Public Works Department watches this thing, and sees that water is not wasted, and that the consumption is carried on, as it ought to be carried on, on business principles. If a watch is maintained the charge will not exceed $7,500. If no charge is kept, one does not know what will happen. No, I beg pardon, that statement does not apply to the leased buildings because the payments for those buildings are upon a taxation basis. It does apply, however, to our own buildings, to Rideau Hall grounds and to the Experimental Farm. Just here I may say I am told that they irrigate land out on the farm with water pumped from the city of Ottawa. That may be necessary, but I do not believe it myself; and when the meter system is installed, as it is going to be if this proposition goes through, I hope there will be somebody to see that they do not irrigate the land at the farm with water pumped by the city. In other words, I hope we can get this thing down to a business basis.
Now, Sir, I have said all that I ought to say on this subject, although I have not said half as much as I would like to. This is a matter the members of the House ought to know something about and to take a hand in, because it affects not only the city of Ottawa but the whole of Canada. Therefore, it is something which members generally ought to take into consideration.

It is very largely the Ottawa attitude-they want it. That is the Ottawa mentality. They want it, and they look upon the Government as being in a sense a source of supply 'from which they can dig up the gold. The gold is there, and they want it-that is all I can say about it.

The city is entitled to be paid for the water consumed by us, and they are entitled to something for the sewers, because our main sewers empty into theirs, and therefore they are entitled to be paid for that convenience. I think $150,000 far too much .for the payment of these services.
It is plenty big enough, anyway.

AIX>
TO PROVINCES EOR HIGHWAY CONSTRUCTION.
On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid (Minister of Railways), Bill No. 152, to encourage the Construction and Improvement of Highways, was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 2-definition:
Under the Provincial Highways Act, bridges are included in highways. This definition does not seem to include bridges,

It includes only culverts and small bridges, not large bridges. For

instance, it would not include such a bridge as the bridge across the Ottawa river between St. Anne and Montreal.
There are small bridges of various sdzesi, and if the minister thinks that small bridges are included it seems to me that the clause should provide where to stop.
Why not state in the Bill that the bridges to be included in the highways shall be of a length of one hundred feet or two hundred feet?
It is not the intention to include bridges unless- they are culverts or small bridges which -are really parts of the road. A bridge of any considerable size would not be included.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-grant of twenty millions:

Before this section carries, without the least desire to delay the House at this period of the session, I want to enter as strong a protest as an individual member can against this legislation. I do that, in the first place, because the legislation, according to legal authority in this House, is a breach of the constitution of this country. The roads are given for the care of the provinces under the British North America Act, and I protest against this as a breach of the Constitution. I object to it, in the second place, because, being a breach of the Constitution, it is an unparalleled and indefensible expenditure of public money on the part of this Government at a time when the finances of our country are strained to the breaking point. I need not elaborate to what extent they are strained; I have dwelt upon it again and again, and the patience of men who have nothing but the good of the country at heart has been strained to the breaking point also by the actions of this Government within the last few days. Money is flung here by the million, there by the ten million, on one day and on the other day; and the next day the Minister of Finance comes before us and in three minutes or four minutes or four hours, as the case may be, gets a -Bill through this House to borrow another hundred millions. We are told that this fall a domestic loan is to be presented to the people. I expressed my opinion in the Budget debate upon the merits of these domestic loans. Let me tell the Government that there are citizens in this country, who have not the same objection in principle that I have to the domestic loans, but

who, nevertheless, purpose abstaining from subscribing to them because they are encouraging this Government to waste money. The Government may like it or not, but the facts are as I state: That citizens all over 'Canada are threatening in private to refuse to subscribe to these loans because the Government is not fit to handle the money that is so raised. Let it be understood, Sir, if I need to explain it, that I have no objection to the improvement of roads; I should be next door to an uncivilized person if I had. Macaulay points out, in the well known portion of his history which deals with the condition of England under Charles II, that the advancement of a country may be estimated roughly by the condition of its- roads, but Macaulay never advised the Imperial Government to do the work of county councils in the matter of roads, and never would have condoned it, and no other English statesman would. I need not say any more. The two objections that I have already raised would be absolutely insurmountable in the minds of a Government that had not divested themselves, apparently, of all public responsibility in the matter of the financial condition of the country. I object, I repeat, to this legislation because in the first place it is unconstitutional, and in the second place, being unconstitutional, it is absolutely reprehensible and utterly indefensible in view of the present condition of the country's finances.

I am in entire accord with the statements so eloquently expressed by my hon. friend (Mr. Clark). I had hoped that the Government, realizing as they must have done before now, the very strong dissent of a number of their supporters on this side of the /House, would have refrained from attempting to advance this legislation at this stage of the session, but apparently, for reasons which no doubt appear to them good, they have determined to force this legislation through, and the only course that remains for me is to express my very strong dissent from the purpose and principle of this legislation.
When the question of Dominion participation in the building of highways was before this House in 1913 and 1914, I supported the legislation. The situation then was very different from' what it is now. On that occasion we had an overflowing treasury, and, comparatively speaking, few demands upon it. The Provincial Governments, relatively speaking, were hard up, and it did seem to me quite reasonable that inasmuch as the Provincial Governments
had not successfully and completely dealt with the problem of good roads, the Federal 'Government might well assist the provinces in this particular work. The proposition made by the Government* at that time provided for the money being expended by the Federal Government; the Opposition took the view that the money should not be expended directly by the Federal Government but handed over to the provinces to expend. The House divided on that question, and the minister who is in charge of this Bill voted with me against the proposition advanced by the Opposition and in favour of the Federal Government expending the money directly, out of the moneys it had received directly from the people of this country. The minister the other evening attempted to show that I should support this resolution because I had voted for the same principle, he said, on two or three other occasions. I contradicted his statement then and I say now that I never voted for any such legislation, and more than that, the minister never voted for any such legislation. We voted for a principle exactly the opposite, and if my .attitude is to be compared with his, so far as consistency is concerned,
I do not think mine will suffer by the comparison. To-day the situation is entirely changed. On previous occasions when this House expressed itself in favour of legislation looking toward the improvement of highways, the Federal Government had an overflowing treasury, and relatively speaking, the Provincial Governments were poor. To-day the positions are exactly reversed. Since the war a great many calls have been made on the Federal treasury, calls greater in magnitude than any one previously supposed could have been borne, and very few calls of an exceptional character have been made on the Provincial Governments. The result is that, relatively speaking, our position is very much inferior to that of the provinces at the present time. Last year this Government floated a loan free of Federal taxes at a higher cost to the Government than five and-a-half per cent. The other day the little province of Nova Scotia was obliged to borrow money, and their ten-year five-per-cent bonds were eagerly snapped up within a point and a fraction of par, or at an interest cost to that province of less than five and one-fifth per cent. I ask any sane man in this House what justification there can be for the Federal Government stepping in at this time and, as my hon. friend (Mr. Clark) has so eloquently said, breaking the constitu-

I am strongly in favour of good roads, and I know itbat there are many hon. members in the House whose desire for good roads is possibly paramount in their minds. But I cannot, having attacked the Government for extravagance, allow criticism of this Bill to come merely from their own side of the House and from the cross benches while I remain silent. I regard this Bill as nothing more nor less than a programme for joy riding Ito bankruptcy. What sort of Toads do we require in. this country above all things? Not large trunk roads for automobilists to enjoy themselves on. They have their value and under another condition of finance in this country they might be permissible. But the roads which are required in this country above everything else are roads that are not more than reasonably expensive and reasonably maintainable, leading from the home of the farmer to 'the cheese factory, the station and the church. These roads are essentially a matter for the rural townships. If you take a road which goes through heavy clay country it will be more expensive than one which goes through gravel country; but the heavy clay country will produce crops far greater than those produced in the light gravelly soil, and therefore the disadvantage in the expense of the one will be offset by the advantage in the greater fertility and strength of soil. It is eminently unfair therefore to place roads on too wide a basis. Another strong point is this: It is essentially unsound for one governing power to raise money and another governing power to spend it.
Confederation imposed that system upon us, but it should be kept within the narrowest possible limits, and I am absolutely opposed to the Dominion Government raising money and handing it over to the provinces to spend. It means one of two things. Either the Dominion Government has to leave the provinces to their - own sweet will in distributing the money, or it will have to see that it is properly distributed and spent. If they take the latter alternative they must duplicate departments; we must have a department of roads for the Dominion and one for the province. In this country, it seems to me, the first necessity is to develop one system of transportation. In the Western Provinces,, I understand, they are much more anxious to have railways than highways at this time, and it is important that public money should be spent on giving means of communication to the whole country before the Dominion Government assists in duplicating means of communication in Eastern 'Canada. We have railways in Eastern Canada, and if we subsidize great arteries of highways they will more or less duplicate the railways. Highways have their value and I trust that no hon. member will accuse me of being ignorant or unappreciative of the fact. I value them in a high degree, but I say that for this Government to spend any money that is not absolutely required, when we have to borrow for everything but the bare cost of administering the affairs of the country, is essentially unwise. I do not wish to repeat what I said in my remarks on the Budget, but I drew attention of the House to this fact, that one of the greatest causes of the high cost of living in Canada was inflation of credit. Borrowing will continue the inflation of credit, and it is a matter which deserves severe condemnation for this Government, in order to please some . people who largely belong to the automo-bilist class, to borrow money, and thus increase the cost of living to the poor widow, the poor workingman, and those who are suffering possibly more than any one else from the high cost of living-the clergyman, the teacher and the man with a small salary which has not kept pace with the increase in the cost of living.
There is one argument that might be brought forward; you say that this will give employment to the people. These gr^at roads will have to be built through the rural districts. There is no lack of, employment in the rural parts; on the contrary, there is a tremendous scarcity of employment there, and it will be a poor benefit to

Canada if you take men from the fields to haul and crush stone for roads when they would be better employed raising wheat, milking cows and doing other such work. On the whole, I believe that this legislation is a mistake. I know that I may incur some unpopularity with some sections of the people by opposing a grant of money for roads, but you can pay too high a price even for a good thing and I wish my protest to be registered against what I consider as a mistaken step by the 'Government in connection with the expenditure of money that is not warranted in the present financial condition of the country.

I regret that at the very first opportunity this Dominion gets of giving a little assistance to the rural population the proposition has met with such opposition. I think the people of this Dominion are well entitled to a grant of this kind, because whenever appropriations have been required 'for railways, harbours, and other public works the representatives of the people of the rural constituencies have always voted for them. When an opportunity comes to this Parliament to vote for a grant of money to improve the roads, a work which is most essential at the present time, the proposition is met by what I might call the small men in the Opposition. If it was proposed to erect a public building in a city it would be all right with them, but when anything is proposed for the general good of the rural population these gentlemen are against it. Talk about the cost of living! There is nothing that will bring down the cost of living to a greater extent than good roads, and there is not a mah throughout the country but who will agree with me as to the great necessity at the present time of improving our highways. There is a little thing I heard outside of this Chamber and that is that there are some politics in the opposition that these hon. gentlemen are offering to this good roads proposition. We ought to get out of that way of looking at a question of this kind; we ought to be bigger men than that. We ought to get it into our heads that the taxes of the Dominion which are spent for this purpose are spent for the general good of the country. We are asked the question: What have we done to build roads? The townships in my county have been building roads for the lasit sixty years and the county which I have the honour to represent is spending $20,000 a year in building roads. The provinces are spending thousands and millions of dollars for roads all over the Dominion. You talk 
about the war. Who contributed to the winning of the war? Did we not all contribute to the funds that were necessary to win the war? My county took the first $50,000 of the Victory Loan. We did not care about roads; we wanted to win the war. The war is now won and we say: Give us good roads. We are not asking for charity; we want to pay our share and we can do it. We have voted for railways, harbours, canals; now we want good roads, and I regret that there should be any objection made to this first grant which the people of the rural constituencies have ever asked to be made for the purpose af assisting in the building of good roads.
iMr. BALDWIN: No man in this House is more interested in good roads than I am. For about fifteen years I have worked for good roads in my county, and I contributed $5,000 from my own pocket to help build eighteen miles of provincial roads. I wanted to spent $1,000 or $2,000 of my own money for the construction of a road in my own county, but the municipal council did not approve of my offer, and therefore the road was not built. I considered that the money would have been well spent because it would have resulted in more traffic with less horsepower, less breakage of wagons and harness.
But owing to the position in which this Dominion stands to-day I must protest against the proposal which is now before the House. In the first place, we have not the money. This is an inopportune time to undertake this project. It is unconstitutional, and besides labour is very scarce in the country. This $20,000,000 would go but a short distance in building roads throughout this Dominion. It has been proven that the Provincial Governments can get money at a lower rate of interest than the Federal Government and so long as this burden is upon the people let us get money from the cheapest source possible and apply it in our own way and under the direction of our own provincial engineers. In so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, it has every facility through its engineers for building good roads without having attached to it any leading strings from this Parliament. There are many reasons for not voting this money when our people are overburdened and when the load is being added to by almost every enactment of this House. I regret that I must protest against this Bill, however much I am in favour of good roads.

I wonder if the minister in that peculiarly lucid manner of his, would now be good enough to explain to

us what he expects to gain financially by having this Dominion borrow money for provincial purposes at a higher rate of interest than that at which the provinces can borrow it for the purpose of extending provincial roads.

I did not wish to be discourteous to the hon. member. If the hon. member would have looked at the time he would have seen that hon. members stood up and I did not have an opportunity of answering him. I had no intention of not replying to his question. I shall do so now. As to his question: What would be gained by the Dominion borrowing money at a higher rate of interest than the provinces will pay? Any person-the hon. member himself-knows that a question of that kind is one that can be easily answered. I cannot see any object to be gained by the Dominion Government borrowing money at a higher rate of interest. But it is my opinion that it will be of great advantage to the people of Canada as a whole to have good roads. I believe that and, believing that, I have put this Bill on the Order Paper. I believe it is the duty of the Dominion to assist the building of good roads throughout the country. Believing that we should assist the building of good roads, then, I believe that we should provide the money, and if we have to borrow it or do it by taxation, whatever the rate of interest is, we have to pay it. Let me say in Tegard to the claim of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), that this is unconstitutional, that he did not say it was unconstitutional when the Dominion Government gave assistance to agriculture, such assistance to be distributed by the local governments. I was only too pleased to vote that the money should be distributed by the local governments subject to the supervision of the Dominion Government in so far as agricultural and technical education is concerned.
As to this measure being unconstitutional neither the legal advisers of my department nor of the Justice Department have given utterance to any such opinion. I do not believe myself that it is unconstitutional to assist in the construction of good roads. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davidson) knows that in regard to provincial railways for which charters were granted by the provincial legislatures and over which this Parliament had no jurisdiction at all, federal subsidies have been granted for years. If it is unconstitutional to assist in building good roads throughout the Dominion it is equally unconstitutional for this Parliament to vote subsidies for the purpose referred to. My own view is that we should give assistance to these undertakings, regardless of whether they are provincial or federal, so long as they are in the interests of the people as a whole, and good roads are undoubtedly of that character.

Does the minister
think, for example, that a road leading from a country town in Ontario to some remote district in the country would be a benefit to the farmers in Saskatchewan?

I believe that a similar road from a city or town in Saskatchewan would be an advantage to the people of that province. In the same way, it i3 my opinion that a road leading from a town in Annapolis to a remote part of the county would be of advantage to the people of that county. Now in the United States the situation is similar to the one we have here in so far as granting aid towards the building of roads is concerned. In the ad. joining republic the ownership of roads is vested in the several states, yet we find Congress voting $260,000,000, or $300,000,000 to be appropriated among the various states for the construction of good roads.
They can afford to do that.

But the United States are borrowing the money for the purpose and it involves taxing the people as a whole. As regards the Canadian situation I am optimistic enough to believe that we can satisfactorily solve our financial problems and provide the necessary money for this purpose. I wish to endorse the statement made by an hon. gentleman in this ddbate that if we are going in for increased production, proper facilities for transportation should be provided. I believe this Bill to be a good one. It is legislation which this Parliament should pass and more than that, the people of the country have already voted in favour of it. They endorsed it in 1911, and in the general elections of 1917 which resulted in the return of the Union Government. The proposition we are asking the House to support was a plank in the Government's platform
Oh, oh.

-and it was endorsed by the people of Canada.
An hqn. MEMBER:	It is highway robbery.

Furthermore, the Bill
was promised in the speech from the

Throne and has been brought up on several previous occasions this session. Personally, I want to hear the views of members with respect to it, but I am not trying to force through a measure unless public sentiment favour it and I certainly consider we have the public behind us in this matter.
We are not.

I do not want any such legislation except it will be in the interest of the people as a whole. Believing that, and holding the view that it will result in improved transportation in every constituency, I submit the Bill for the consideration of this committee.

It is very
late in the session for such legislation.

The minister has reminded
us that this legislation was promised in the speech from the Throne, yet he only brings it forward in the dying hours of a somewhat long and tiresome session.
The Bill has been up before; it has been considered two or three times.
Merely as a matter of form. Mr. J. D. REID:	No, it has been discussed by the House on several occasions.

The first to speak upon the Bill, after it was presented to us, was an hon. gentleman who has loyally supported the present Government. He tells the Government he has reached the conclusion, or that many people throughout the country have reached the conclusion, that the Government is not fit to expend the public money, that it is not to be trusted.
They are unfit.

The next speaker was the
assistant chief whip, who opposed the resolution in a lengthy speech. Have we therefore not reason to ask ourselves whether the Government is serious, and what the conditions are throughout the country, when two of the most active supporters of the Administration from the time the Union Government was formed, get up this morning and condemn this legislation? I submit it is high time the country should have a statement from-the Prime Minister in order to ascertain whether the Government is serious in respect to this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend has said that this Bill has been left over until the closing hours of this session.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend must recall the fact that the minister has presented the measure to the House on two or three previous occasions, and each time a lengthy discussion took place upon it. The House has had full opportunity of discussing the matter at much earlier stages of the session than the present.
However, I rose for the purpose of speaking on one or two aspects of the matter. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) spoke very strongly against the Bill and expressed his surprise that the Government should introduce such a measure. Let me tell him that one of the reasons it has been introduced is that it formed part of the platform and policy of the Union Government when that Government was formed. The fact was so stated and announced to the people of Canada by the Prime Minister when he published the basis upon which the present Government was formed. Let me read a paragraph from the statement which was issued by the Prime Minister on the 18th October, 1917, outlining the policies which the Union Government was created to put into effect. Paragraph 7 of that statement reads as follows:
7. The development of transportation facilities; the co-operative management of the various railway systems, so as to ensure economy in operation, to avoid unnecessary construction, and to secure the widest and most effective use of existing railway facilities;
That has been carried out, so far as is practicable at the present time, by the creation of the board to manage all the railway systems under Government control, and will be carried out further when the Government secures the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific railways .
It will take some money.

Then oomes the fourth proposal:
The investigation of the possibilities of the air service for important national purposes.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When the committee rose at one o'clock, I had just concluded a reference to the statement issued by the Prime Minister at the time of the formation of the Union Government indicating the policy which tfhe Union Government proposed to follow. In introducing this Bill, therefore, the Government is but carrying out the pledge it made ito the country at that time.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) raised a question as to the constitu-' tionali'ty of the proposed measure. I do not. know upon what basis my hon. friend questioned its constitutionality. It is quite clearly within the competence of the Federal Parliament to pass an Act of this
kind and to render assistance to the provinces in the construction or maintenance of good roads within the provinces. I can see that there might be objection on the grounds urged by my hon. friend if the Government proposed, against the wish of the provinces, to construct highways within the provinces. But that is not proposed by this Bill; no action can be taken under the Bill without the full consent and approval of the province. Since the committee rose I have ascertained that at the interprovincial conference the question was considered and my information is that there was no dissent; indeed, those present ' were heartily in favour of the proposal.
My hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) has raised the general question whether one Government should raise moneys for another Government to spend. That subject was discussed prior to Confederation, and a great deal may be said in favour of the suggestion that one Government should not raise moneys and turn them over to another to expend. But whatever our views may be on this question, the Fathers of Com federation have settled this matter for us. It is too late for us to attempt to decide matters on that basis. By the British North America Act large revenues received by the provinces prior to Confederation were turned oveT to the Dominion and provision was made to compensate the provinces by subsidies paid from the Federal Treasury. From time to time these subsidies have been received and the amounts increased in order to enable the provinces to carry on the various branches of the public service which are committed to them under the British North America Act. Therefore, I think we must approach the consideration of the matter absolutely on its merits, irrespective of any constitutional objection such as the member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) has raised, and irrespective of the objection urged by the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). The question, therefore, if considered on its merits, is this: Is it in the national interest that the Government of Canada should assist in constructing and improving and maintaining the highways of Canada? If it is a matter of purely local and domestic concern, it might be fairly and strongly argued that the Parliament of Canada should not take up the proposition. But I think it is difficult to argue successfully that the matter of good roads is one of purely local and domestic concern. I submit the matter of good roads throughout the country is one of the most important

that we can be called upon to consider in the interests of the general improvement and development of the whole country. These roads connect up with our railway systems of transportation; they are the only means of communication between the homes of thousands-yes, of millions-of our people and the various centres of population; therefore, a good system of highways throughout the country is of great national moment. Moreover, good roads will contribute to the public welfare by increasing the comfort and convenience of the people in our rural sections and, I venture to say, will help to keep the people on the farm and therefore increase production. In a word, good roads would generally improve the conditions of rural life in Canada, as they have improved the conditions of rural life in every country where good roads have been built. I submit, therefore, that the matter of good roads is one of national concern in which the Federal Government may properly take an interest, having regard to the welfare, progress and prosperity of all the people of Canada. The Bill, therefore, can be justified on that ground.
Then, we come to the last point which was expressed so strongly by the member for Red Deer, and that is the question of spending the money at the present time. To my mind, that is really the one serious aspect of the question. On every other ground, the proposal is so obviously in the public interest that its merits should secure the unanimous endorsation of the House; but I quite agree that it is a fair matter for debate whether, in view of the conditions arising out of the war, we should expend so large a sum of money on good roads at this time. While recognizing the important considerations which the member for Red Deer has presented to the Committee, the Government reached the conclusion-which was announced in the speech from the Throne and which is implemented by this Bill-that it was in the public interest that assistance should be given to the good roads movement as part of the plan of national development. There are two things which we must keep in mind. Our large debt constitutes a serious burden upon the people. The only way we can successfully meet the situation is by increasing national production. We can contribute toward this end by improving the conditions of rural life and thus offering larger inducements for the people to stay on or return to the farm. Any increase in national production makes us 
more capable to bear the national burdens. I agree that we should not embark upon unproductive expenditures at this time. There is necessity for economy and for thrift; the Canadian people will probably have to learn a good deal more of thrift and economy before we are relieved from the burden of debt which this war has put upon us.
And the Canadian Government.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, that may be a matter for debate, too. But I submit that any proper expenditure that increases the productive power of the people increases also our ability to carry the burden of debt and ultimately pay it off. On that ground I think we can justify this public expenditure, as well as on the further ground, which was an important consideration in a number of the proposals the Government has made this session,-that it is wise to provide employment during the period of reconstruction following the war. The Government felt it incumbent to adopt such measures as were within its power to promote the construction of public works and undertakings of a productive character in order that such employment should be provided. The building of roads at this time should assist in providing that necessary employment. For these reasons I submit that the Bill introduced by the Minister of Railways is not against the public interest, but is in the public interest and is deserving the support of the House.

Before sitting down will my hon. friend apply himself to the solution of a problem which I propounded, with somewhat indifferent success I am afraid, to the Minister of Railways, namely: How can he justify on the grounds of good business the Federal Government borrowing money at a higher rate of interest than the provinces pay, to be handed over to the provinces to be expended by them on a purely provincial matter.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend must certainly have misunderstood what I said. I did not say the constitution must take second place. I said that this legislation was not contrary to the constitution, But quite within the constitution.

I say that it is quite without the constitution; that is where I take exception to my hon. friend's argument. We know that one of the planks of Toryism is centralization. You begin by saying: We will grant money to the provinces, or we will loan them money. Then after you have inserted the thin end of the wedge you will run the whole thing. When the question of technical education was before the House we pointed out the dangers of the Federal Parliament touching such subjects. I claim that every matter which has been made a subject of exclusive provincial legislation ought to be left to the provinces. My hon. friend (Mr. Rowell) says the provinces will expend the money. But the provinces have to enter into an agreement with the Dominion Government, and that is the stick this Government will hold over them. This Government has the right to say what kind of a road shall be built, what the specifications shall be, and in what part of the country Che road shall be built. It is all very well to say that it will be done by agreement, but if one of the parties does not consent to the agreement there will be no agree-
As they should be.

My hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) says " as they should be," and I share his view. I do not see why they should be exempt, because I am in favour of imposing a tax upon every kind of income, no matter from where it may come. What interest can he put on these bonds that will not prejudicially affect them upon the market?
Five per -cent.

Five per cent? It will more likely be six or seven per cent. If the bonds are taxable the response of the true patriot is going to shrink in direct ratio to the reduction of the benefit he is going to get from the bonds. It has been said, and rightly said, in this House that to-day these Victory loan bonds are finding their way into the hands of the man who has the capital. That man will get up and sing patriotic songs but he will try and get as much of his income behind the Victory and the Liberty bonds as he can member of this Parliament, say "no." The fortunate enough-no, it is not my misfortune-to belong to the millionaire class and therefore my income tax does not come from Victory Bonds because I cannot buy them. But if the people are going to ask the question: What are you going to use [DOT] this money for, and if the Government are going to take the ground that they are going to use the money they have to borrow for the simple purpose of trying to throw a bait out to the provinces, because the provinces want to build roads, I, as a member of this Parliament say "no." The provinces are well able to build their own roads. I do not think there is a province in the Dominion that has not as good credit as the Dominion has and if the people of those provinces are so anxious about building roads, if they have to pay back the money to the Dominion, because they will have to be taxed to pay it back, let them go down in their own pockets, pay the tax to the province and let the privileges, rights and powers of the various provinces and of the Dominion be respected as defined by the constitution.
I do not see any good reason for bringing in this Bill at this time, but, on the contrary I see every reason for protecting the credit of the country, helping along the business of the country, and giving the country confidence that we will be able to legislate seriously and that we will not do anything that will mean throwing away the money that we have to borrow to meet the deficit. Let us show by the legislation that we pass in this House that we do not want to do anything but that which is absolutely necessary and of primary importance to the welfare of this country.
I admit the desirability of having good roads all over the country not only for transportation purposes but for many other reasons. My reason for favouring the construction of good roads extends beyond the mere question of transportation. If we 
have good roads all over the Dominion we will have harmony and good feeling. Good roads mean travel and travel permits intercourse between individuals. I am satisfied that if we had good roads between Three Rivers and Toronto the people of Toronto would motor down to Three Rivers and see what nice people we are.
You might have an Orange lodge there.

We might have an Orange lodge there and there is nothing to prevent it. I am quite willing to learn all the good that there is in other people. I speak from the bottom of my heart when I say that I am wholly and entirely in favour of good roads and that I think good roads are essential to the welfare of the people. But I think a man makes a mistake who builds a $20,000 house when he has only $10,000 because if he goes bankrupt upon it those who are depending upon him and those who come after him will get no benefit from it. The reasons advanced by the President of the Privy Council in support of this proposal are not sufficient to convince me. The work which will be given to the soldier will not last for more than a month, winter will set in and the work will be over. Another reason why I oppose this vote is that I do not want my hon. friends on this side of the House, after the next election, and when they go over to the other side, to be saddled with this $20,000,000 and, if they are saddled with it, I want them to be able to explain it and to give good reasons for it. That is one of the reasons why I do not want to support this measure. It does not appear to-day that we have the means to carry out this proposal and therefore I oppose it.

If the last reason advanced by my friend (Mr. Bureau) were the only reason, it would not be necessary for any person to take up the question further. I do not think he need worry about 'the responsibility which will fall upon him and his colleagues on the other side of the House when they are sitting on this side of the House because I do not think it will be in the very near future.
It will be in the new buildings, not here.

According to the last reports, the progress is not rapid on the new Parliament Buildings so that anyhow it will be some time in the future before gentlemen opposite have to assume responsibility for Government. My hon. friend has accepted the constitutionality of

this Act, and if I caught his words correctly, he said: "No conditions would make him ignore the Constitution." It seems to me that if we were to hand this money over to the provinces to be expended by them as we would stipulate for the building or improvement of roads, it would be open to the same objection from the constitutional standpoint as if we gave forty per cent and. had a written or some other kind of agreement with the provinces as to how the money should be expended.
I admit that but it would not have a political string to it.
If my hon. friend admits that handing it over to the province is open to objection which he raises from a constitutional standpoint-
For the specific purpose of roads.
-for the specific purpose, certainly, of improving the roads, then my hon. friend is in the position a little later on of saying that he is willing to hand that over to the provinces.
As an increased subsidy.
As an increased subsidy for a specific purpose.
No; not for a specific purpose.

That specific purpose being the improvement of roads. My hon. friend is on record not only to-day but he is on record several years ago as voting in favour of handing money over to the provinces for the specific purpose of improving or building roads.
Back in 1912 my hon. friend put himself on record on this question, and he did the same in 1S13. On both occasions my hon. friend, when he supported and spoke in favour of the amendment proposed by the Senate-which amendment did not oppose the Federal Government giving the money to the provinces bu't desired the handing of it over rbo the provincial governments to be used for the specific purpose of building and improving roads-had with him the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) and many others, who were members of Parliament at that time and still occupy seats in this House. On the occasion referred to, the hon. gentleman (Mr. M. Clark) did not raise the question of the unconstitutionality of the policy. Neither he nor the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) objected to the principle of the Federal Government spending money for
27&i
the purpose. On the contrary, the former was very strongly in favour of the policy. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Michael Clark) said:
We would like these roads, There is no reason why the Government should not accept the amendment.
That was the amendment of the Senate which proposed to hand the money over to the provinces. To-day, one of the strong arguments of the hon. gentleman, advanced with a good deal of vigour, is that the policy is unconstitutional, and in that respect he is backed up by the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson). Sir Wilfrid Laurier did not raise the question of the policy being unconstitutional in 1912 or in 1913. I have glanced over the debates in both years and I do not find that any person on either side raised such a question. There was a difference of opinion then, as there is a difference of opinion now, as to whether the money should be handed over to the provinces, permitting them to use their own judgment in the matter so long as it was expended on roads. That position was- taken in 1912 and 1913 by a number of hon. gentlemen who still sit in this House. Sir Wilfrid Laurier did not then, object to the Federal Government assisting the provinces in regard to the building and improvement of highways. He wanted the money handed over to>
the provincial governments without the Federal Government having any voice in the matter further than to say that the money voted by this Parliament must be expended for the purpose designated. I supported the Bill that, was introduced in 1912, and again in 1913, for the building and improvement of highways. That Bill provided that we should have a say in the expenditure of the money, and I have on previous occasions maintained that 'that is a position we cannot afford to recede from. I say that if this Parliament votes money for technical education, or for agriculture, or for good roads, or for any other specific purpose, and certainly for a purpose which may be regarded as purely provincial, we are responsible for the voting of that money, and we should have some say as 'to what is being done with it.
Hear, hear.

And we should follow up our vote in the manner indicated. I confess to you, Mr. Chairman, that I entertain some doubt in regard to the Bill as it is now. Let me repeat, I am strongly in favour of federal assistance for improving our high-

ways. I believe that can be justified and justified up to the hilt. I believe it is in the general interests of Canada that money should be spent in assisting the provinces to improve the highways. But what causes me to have some suspicion is that the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) remains silent while this matter is going through. The leader of the Opposition also remains silent, and I am suspicious of the silence of both hon. gentlemen.
Oh, oh.

Yes, the question of politics has come up in connection with this matter, and I want to confess that I for one am suspicious of the silence of those hon. gentlemen. If their acceptance of this Bill means that the various Provincial Governments are to have control of the expenditure of the money and the Dominion Government will virtually have no voice in it, I say that is something which would be regrettable.
Speaking on the matter the other night, I made a suggestion which I think is worthy of consideration. Different hon. gentlemen have raised the question of politics. The hon. member for Three Rivers was suspicious that this money would be used for political purposes. I contend, Sir, that in voting this money it is the duty of Parliament, as far as it possibly can, to safeguard its expenditure in order to prevent the money being used by any Provincial Government for political purposes, and T believe that can be done.
How can it be done?

The money which we propose to' vote for the construction and improvement of highways should be spent on the higher class of road, a standard road, a road which will be decided upon by the provincial and Dominion engineers as being of a certain class. Very well, let that be stipulated, so that the money shall not be devoted to the improvement of back concession lines. Let it be specified that these highways must be of a certain standard. Having fixed your standard for them there should likewise be a guarantee that the contract would be let by tender. When you are building fifteen, twenty, or fifty miles of road, it is a very simple matter, if your engineers have agreed upon the standard of road to be built for that distance, to let, for.example, five miles by tender, and the lowest bidder will get the contract. When that happens the contractor is going to

secure his labour wherever he can get it regardless of how those people vote, and I believe that is something provision should be made for in this Bill. To illustrate my point further: Where the money goes to the province of Ontario-and there we have a government in office which we know would not abuse its rights, which would deal properly with this money and would not use it for any ulterior purpose-in view of the fact that the federal authorities are contributing forty per cent of the money, going towards the construction of' a highway, we have a right to say to the Government of Ontario: " Bring on your engineers now and we will have our engineers consult with them as to the standard of road to be built, and you must agree to let the contract for that piece of road by tender "-not hand the money over to the province and let it carry out the work by day's labour. I can see that if the money were handed over without conditions there might be a very great deal of danger, no matter in what province the money may be expended. Every member who has spoken on this subject agrees that we want good roads in the general interest of the country. There is no question about that. Every one here, it seems to me, should be willing to agree that so far as this money is concerned there should be no suspicion of its being used in any province for political purposes. I repeat, we can avoid that by making it a part of the contract that the building of the road must be let by tender, and in that way we will take the matter entirely out of politics.
One hon. gentleman asked of what benefit would it be to the farmers of Saskatchewan or Alberta to build a piece of road in the province of Ontario. We might put the question in this way:	Of what benefit will it be to the farmers of Ontario to build the Hudson's Bay railway; or to build a line of railway out to a settlement in the West which at present is forty or fifty miles away from a railway? I contend, Sir, that it would be a benefit to the farmers of Ontario that the producers in any part of Saskatchewan should have a better opportunity to get their goods to market. I contend that it would be to the interest of the farmers of Saskatchewan if by building good roads and improving the transportation facilities of the farmers of Ontario we add to the wealth of those farmers-and we certainly will-for that is something which is for the general benefit of the Dominion.
I am very strongly in favour of the Federal Government assisting the provinces, and especially the older provinces, in re-

gard to the building of highways. The older provinces have played a big part and have -made big sacrifices in the development of the newer portions of the country. The people of the eastern part of Canada rejoice in the prosperity of those of the West. But we have difficulties to face here, and one of the heaviest burdens resting upon the farming community of Ontario is the keeping up of their roads. Twice the money that was used ten or fifteen years ago in maintaining out roads in fairly good condition will not suffice to-day; it is an utter impossibility. Not only is this consideration justly due to the rural districts of Ontario, but I repeat that, in my opinion, an improvement in our roads in Ontario or Quebec or in any other province is not merely something for the welfare of the province in which the money is spent, but something which will be for the welfare of Canada as a whole.
Let me repeat once more before I sit down, that I do thjnk this Bill should contain a stipulation that the money voted by this House is to be voted on the understanding that it will be spent in the way I have suggested-by letting the work out to tender instead of handing the money over to the provinces to spend on day work.

Mr. Chairman, the Committee has had a speech from my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council of very great moderation. I could not help thinking that his moderation was in proportion to his own consciousness of the weakness of his case, because I have heard my hon. friend speak with very much greater vigour-always with courtesy, I admit, but with very much greater vigour -than he did in the speech which he has just delivered. On the question of the constitutionality of this measure, I am afraid I should display very great temerity if I entered into a legal argument with my hon. friend, who is not only a member of this Cabinet but a lawyer of ability. However, I have been reading the section of the British North America Act which deals with this question, and I have come to the conclusion that this procedure is of very doubtful constitutionality. We should settle a question of constitutionality, usually, I think, in the first place, according to law, and in the second place, according to precedent. I think I should be on sound ground in thinking that the constitutionality of our procedure would base itself upon those two considerations.
With regard to the law, I am prepared to contend, until some legal authority corrects me, that the only highway which would come under clause 10 of the 4 p.m. section of the British North America Act which deals with matters exclusively within the rights of the provinces, would be a highway connecting one province with another; in other words, an interprovincial or national highway. Because, while railways and telegraph lines and other things are mentioned specifically, the only possibility of getting highways within that clause is under the phrase " other works connecting one province with another." Now, I want to put a question to my hon. friend (Mr. Rowell): In his support of this Bill does he contemplate an interprovincial highway? I do not need to wait for the answer, because he has told us specifically that the highways in his mind are the highways within the province which would be of use to the farmer in getting his stuff to market, and in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, nay, in nine hundred and ninety-nine cases out of a thousand, those would not be highways leading from one province to another.
. As to precedent, I am surely on very strong ground. Confederation reached the fifty-second anniversary of its birth yesterday, and the fact that this legislation is before us is conclusive proof, if proof were needed, that for the whole period of Confederation our highways have been exclusively attended to by the provinces. So that on the ground of the law itself, so far as a layman may dare to interpret it, and certainly on the .ground of precedent, I venture to put my opinion very, very humbly and with very much diffidence against the opinion of the hon. the President of the Privy Council.
- Now, my hon. friend from Frontenac (IMr. Edwards) has advanced an argument by which, I think, he endeavoured to fasten a charge of inconsistency in regard to this very matter upon myself and upon other hon. gentlemen sitting to your left, Mr. Chairman. Well, Sir, I may be very obtuse upon the point, but it seems to me that the facts adduced by the hon. gentleman prove exactly the opposite. The Senate amendment, devised in consultation no doubt with the great constitutionalist and the great statesman who at that time was leading the Liberal party, was devised for the very purpose of meeting the constitution. No one has argued that money cannot be given to the provinces by the Federal Government. We give it for a dozen purposes; the whole matter of provincial subsidies proves that. After the

money has been given to the provinces, unless it is especially ear-marked, they can use it for any ourpose, and, as a matter of fact, I presume they do in some cases use it for roads.
There is no contention about that; the contention is aJbout the right of the Federal Government to go into a province and look after what is a provincial work, what has been a provincial work during the whole of the period of Confederation, and what is contemplated as a provincial work by the British North America Act. That is the case so far as my hon. friend is concerned. With regard to that matter, I might say that as to what was proposed to be done five years ago and what is proposed to be done to-day, the whole thing depends upon the method of the doing of it so far as the constitution is concerned. But so far as common sense policy is concerned; so far as a decent national policy is concerned, the whole thing depends on whether or not you have the money to do the thing you are proposing. At that time, owing, of course, to the fact that we had been pursuing a normal course of development and wealth production in this Dominion and had not the obligations of a great war upon our shoulders, it was well within our financial ability to spend the money. But I do not think the most optimistic Canadian will stand up to-day and say that it is well within our ability to follow such a policy now.
Now, why is it essentially a local work and why is it so contemplated? For the very purpose of avoiding the trouble that will arise under this measure. For what does the measure propose? It proposes a double control in regard to a provincial work. That it is still regarded by the Government as a provincial work is demonstrated beyond all possibility of contradiction by the fact that the money is to be given provincially in certain amounts and that the provinces are to be asked to cooperate. The constitution and the precedents followed in this country have been wise constitutions and precedents because they have avoided that double control; they have avoided the interlocking of machinery which would be extremely awkward in practice. It is because of these difficulties that we are opposing this legislation. Under what was proposed by the Senate amendment, to which my hon. friend has referred, there would have been no interlocking of machinery; there would have been no double control. Each province would have done what it has done at all

times-looked after the roads within its own borders, having accepted its share of federal help for the purpose.
We are told by the President of the Council that, the Government does not propose to do anything without the consent of the various provinces. Very well, I am going to put a case, not upon constitutionality, but upon a question of justice. We have not had the information, I contend, that we should have had from the minister in charge of this Bill; and that is one of the reasons why I think we should vote against it if it comes to a vote. We have not had the information which we should have had as to the exact attitude of the Provincial Governments. The Minister of Railways, before he introduces a departure from the practice of Confederation from the beginning up to the present time, should be able to give us exact, tabulated information, on paper, concerning the arrangements that he is proposing to enter into with the various Provincial Governments. We ought to have had information by letter of the consent of these Governments, but we have not that information
I am going to suppose a case. I am going to suppose that some of the provinces do not avail themselves of this Act. The point has been made before, but it is so important that I venture to make it again. Is it not contrary to the spirit of common justice that, at this time, when every part of the country is bearing its own burden, the provinces which, for reasons best known to themeselves, do not take advantage of the supposed benefits of this Act, should be taxed to pay the interest on money which is borrowed to carry this Act into effect for the sake of other provinces? That is travesty on common justice, and I am surprised at that situation being viewed with comparative calm and apparent self-complacency by ministers and members from the "banner" province of Ontario. In the absence of exact information we can only guess, or depend upon inexact information, as to what is the attitude of the provinces. A number of members from the province of Quebec tell us that roads are getting on very well in that province; that the Provincial Government is making a splendid job of its roads; and travellers in that province tell us the same thing. I venture, with very great humility, to offer my compliments to the province of Quebec on setr ting an example to the rest of the Dominion in that particular.
Nova Scotia is in a splendid financial position, according to the evidence of the member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson)-

thanks to the efforts, in no small degree, of the member for iShelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), who, I think, every one down there admits did an immense . work before he came into federal politics for the financial position of Nova iScotia. Well, if Nova Scotia is in that splendid position and some of the most prominent members from Nova Scotia, one of them being a Government whip, do not approve of this legislation, on what principle can we conclude that the province of Nova Scotia is going to come to this Government and seek this help? If they are, it must be in accordance with their Scottish origin; they must not like to pass a good thing, even if they do not need it; they must be imbued with the quality of the Scotchman who keeps the Sabbath and everything else he can lay his hands on. Nova Scotia, therefore, is financially in a good condition; they are doing their provincial business in a good way, and ' I do not think there is any great outcry from that province.
As to New Brunswick, we have a minister from that province who, perhaps, may be heard from in this debate. According to the votes of the last few days, I should say that New Brunswick has a considerable appetite for public money and I should not be surprised to hear that they are ready to receive a little help in regard to their roads.
In the West there has been no great outcry for the expenditure of this money. If It is considered that there has been an outcry in British 'Columbia . that [DOT]conclusion is not, in my judgment, based upon a very careful consideration of their political history; it has rather sprung from what I would call political habit. British Columbia has a history in regard to the building of roads. There was an administration in that province which did very little else but build roads and which was returned to office again and again on its roads policy. In fact, they carried their policy of good roads and their building of roads so far that it was an exceedingly difficult thing to beat them for a great many years; people who went through that province told us that the Government had almost a majority of the voters employed upon the roads-. But the time came when the money would go no further for that sort of business; they rather ran out of the funds that were necessary to carry on that particular line of politics and provincial development -and we know what happened to the Administration in question. Well, I should mot think that that history is one which
would incline hon. gentlemen from British Columbia to be too strong in their advocacy of a roads policy.
In regard to the Prairie Provinces, I think we stand to benefit the least of any, because our roads are not permanent; they are not macadamized; they are mostly made by the farmers on routes contiguous to their own farms. They are trails rather than roads, and I do not suppose that under this Act there is any prospect of their being very rapidly made otherwise. Well, it comes to this: That the main support of this proposition is from Ontario, which is a very great province and rejoices in being known as the "banner province'' of the Dominion. But if Ontario comes to us urging us strongly to pass a roads Bill for its special benefit -what one might call an "Ontario Roads Relief Bill"-then I should really be inclined to follow up the attack upon titles by removing that term "banner" from the title of the province of Ontario.
The President of the Council made his first argument in favour of this scheme upon the policy upon which he alleges- and I think correctly, according to what he read-that the Dominion Government was returned to power. But we in this House are not dependent upon the printed copy of something that was said by the Prime Minister in the last election for our knowledge of the policy upon which the Government were returned to power. If you ask the people of this country what was the policy of this Government that won at the last election, they would answer that, so far as they followed public affairs, the Union Government was returned to power on a policy of winning the war by contributing our last man-yesi, and our last dollar. That was the policy upon 'which 'the Government were returned to power. Even if we admit that good roads were included, a sound financial thing from the point of view of fulfilling the programme of the last election would be *o get after that last dollar before we begin to build roads on borrowed money. I put it to my hon. friend that one of the main planks in the Government's platform had better be carried out before we borrow money by the hundred million to fulfil what was a very minor promise of the Prime Minister and was not in the minds of the people of this country to any great extent at the last election.
I never heard of it in Alberta; I am confident it was not much heard of in Quebec; it might have been vsed in some of the constituencies of Ontario. That is all I have to say about the redemption of

My hon. friend says,
" hear, hear." Let us see. Roads lead off the farm as well as on to it, and supposing that the men in the cities and the returned soldiers have no great taste for roadwork; who is going to do it? Many hon. members in debating this question have made themselves responsible for the opinion that returned soldiers will not go on the roads. .Well, if they don't, and if they won't- and I rather agree with the opinion-then iwho will go? There is only one answer. It will be the men who otherwise would be working on the farms, and I want to draw that consideration to the attention of the acute mind of the President of the Privy Council. I am not content to base .myself upon an opinion in this matter.
