In a very excellent Sunday newspaper, the *Toronto Sunday World, which I suppose gives a general support to the Government, .and which my hon. friend knows well, there *appeared an article last Sunday headed '' Exodus from the Farms," or words to that effect, in which the writer went on to say that one of the results of the housing scheme and the roadwork that this Government is proposing was that it was taking men from production, and not sending .them to it.
That is a very serious statement, made in a journal of repute and only on Sunday last, and I think it is worthy of my hon. friend's consideration. As a matter of fact, if there will be good money going on the roads, instead of the making of good roads helping to increase production it is calculated to have the opposite effect. It is calculated not to form the last step of the country-bound traveller going to agricultural pursuits, but'the first step of the man who is already in agriculture going to the larger wages in the different classes of pursuits and finding himself at last in the over-congested areas of our great cities. I put that to my hon. friend seriously, and give him the source of my information. That article expatiated upon the fact that the rural population of Ontario has been diminishing because of the attractions that there are in the cities for agricultural people.
Would you not have exactly the same result if the province did the work without Federal assistance?

That would not be in my purview. I am not speaking in a Provincial Legislature. I am dealing with the policy of the Government. My hon. friend knows that in the province of Saskatchewan, as well as in Alberta, a great deal of the road work is done by men on the farms for their own convenience under the old system of road making.
I have dealt, I think, with every argument that has been advanced by the ministers in defence of this case. I have dealt with the supposed inconsistencies of myself and others, raised by my hon. friend from Fron-tenac, and I only want to repeat in conclusion that I think that the Government that proposes this expenditure and this borrowing of money at the present time is almost lost to all sense of financial responsibility. I believe the policy is unconstitutional. It is not calculated to increase production, and will not afford employment for returned soldiers. In fact, if I ransacked my intelligence, such as it is, for a single argument by which I could support the proposition, my cerebral tissues would not supply that argument.

My hon. friend from Red Deer seems anxious to know what the Minister of Public Works thinks about this matter, and what the views are of the people in the province of New Brunswick. 1 can tell him in very plain language where I stand upon the question. I am more in favour of this vote for the improvment of highways than for any other Bill which has been submitted to the House of Commons during the present session, and when I say that I am representing the people of New Brunswick to the extent, I believe, of nine-tenths, or perhaps a greater proportion. My hon. friend has paid me a very high compliment in the assertion that he thinks I have tried to realize the financial situation and to face it. I hope I have done so. I have referred to the financial situation a number of times during the present session, and I think I view it as gravely as he does. Nor have I forgotten the somewhat backhanded compliment he gave me in regard to the money being voted for New Brunswick. I shall not enter into the question of constructing public buildings in small or in great localities. Probably that matter will be discussed when my Estimates come down and when there will be an opportunity for discussion. I want to say, however, that as regards any money that has been voted by this Parliament for New Brunswick during this session or last session, I have no apologies whatever to offer. Apart from moneys for the development of the second greatest

seaport in Canada, moneys which are absolutely justifiable under any circumstances, there have been only a few thousand dollars, a mere bagatelle, devoted to that province. My hon. friend says that his own constituency has got nothing, and it may interest him to know that although I have been Minister of Public Works for nearly a year and nine months there has never been one dollar expended in my constituency. I have not asked for a dollar during the year. I endeavour to keep the question of the expenditure of money entirely divorced from any personal feeling, and I know that- there are members who have felt that they have not received what they would like to get for their constituencies. It has been a very unpleasant task for me, but I have tried to deal with every person absolutely upon his merits, regardless of the province or portion of Canada he might represent. My hon. friend submitted a long argument-and what I am about to say replies also to the hon. member for Annapolis-concerning the question of constitutionality. He said that this grant is unconstitutional. I cannot agree with that proposition for a moment. It is true that the British North America Act provides that local works are to be relegated to the provinces. I have not the Act before me, but I am familiar with its provisions, and I would point out to my friend that it is an easy matter to get around that Act. All you need do is to declare a work to be for the general advantage of Canada and you come within the provisions of the Act. So that if it is only a question of constitutionality, that is a trifle. Perhaps my hon. friend is not aware that works of all kinds in the Dominion since 1867- roads, bridges, and everything else-have been declared for the general advantage of Canada, and" the moment that is done they come within the purview of section 92 of the British North America Act.
Except roads.

Yes, roads too. Money has been expended upon roads: and there are members from the province of Quebec who probably may vote against this:-I do not know-and who have been most insistent during the last year that I should bring down appropriations to build roads in Quebec. I had dozens of letters from them, and I have had delegations before me from Quebec of forty or fifty men who have travelled three hundred or four hundred miles for the purpose of convincing me that the Federal Government should build roads in Quebec. This Government

has spent $400,000 in building a road right outside the city of Montreal and we have to. spend a great deal more on it before it is completed. I refer to Laprairie Dike.
Did that road not traverse Government property?

No it went over private property. I may tell my hon. friend that representatives of the late Lieutenant Governor of Quebec want me to pay them a very large amount of money they have taken from that estate. It is just as well for us to have a show-down on some of these things sometimes. No one has been so persistent for the expenditure of money on roads as have been many of the members from Quebec. I will not say all of them, but a great many. I do not think, therefore, that I need spend more time on the constitutionality of the question, because I do not think it enters into the- discussion. It is purely a matter of policy whether or not, under present conditions, Parliament is justified in voting $4,000,000 a year for the next five years to assist in the construction of roads in the various provinces. My friends might sustain an argument on constitutionality if - the proposal were that the Federal Government should go into the province and build a road such as we have done in the case of Laprairie Dike and such as we have done in the eastern por- . tion of Quebec in years gone by. But that is not the proposal. The proposal is that the Government should grant to the provinces forty per cent of the cost of permanent roads which will be built by the provinces according to plans and specifications, the locations to be approved of by this Government. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways this morning answered as completely as any one possibly could the argument in regard to constitutionality when he asked if this be unconstitutional, how it was that we have been granting subsidies to railways for the last forty years- local railways, created by the provinces, which are absolutely local matters. No one raised a question and we can do it again in the case of highways, and nobody can legally or successfully raise a contention. It is a question of policy, I admit, and the question is: Is it good policy or not? I realize that there has been a great change in the financial condition of the country in the last four years, and I take it as a compliment from the hon. member for Red Deer, when that gentleman says that I realize-the fact. I do realize it, and I know that we could do things four years ago that would be rather serious matters

to-day. As I say, I realize our position financially, and also that of the provinces.
I do not agree with some members on the other side of the House and possibly not with some of my colleagues. I do not believe the provinces are in the splendid financial condition that some members seem to think they are. I know the credit of the provinces is good as I know the credit of the Dominion is good. I am glad to learn that the good old province of Nova Scotia was able to float five per cent bonds at a little better than par but that does not say that the Dominion of Canada can float five per cent bonds at better than par. When the provinces came into the Confederation they were given a certain proportion of the total revenues of this country, somewhere about, I think, twenty or twenty-five per cent. Somewhere about twenty-five per cent of the revenue was handed over to the provinces as a subsidy because the provinces gave up to the Dominion their rights to collect revenue from excise and customs' which were the two principal sources of revenue at that time. Things have gone on and these subsidies have been increased only to a very small extent. Instead of getting twenty-five per cent of the total revenues of the Dominion the provinces are not getting five per cent of the total revenues. While the Dominion of Canada has been able to multiply its revenues over and over again the provinces' revenue from the Dominion has practically remained stationary. While the demands on the provincial treasury have increased just the same as the demands on the Dominion treasury have increased the provinces have been compelled to resort to all sorts of methods of levying taxation. Some of the provinces have taken up the question of a direct income tax and now the Dominion Government has been forced to invade that field. I say "forced" advisedly because the Dominion Government cannot do anything else but invade that field. We are taking away a certain measure or taxation which has been open to the provinces and I say here to-day and I say it seriously that the Dominion income tax is here to stay. All that makes it harder for the provinces to finance. I do not agree with many of the members when they say that the provinces are in a much better position to raise financial assistance to construct their roads than the Dominion is.
We had a gathering in this city in the month of December last in the shape of an interprovincial conference. There are no minutes of the conference because the conference did not take votes or come to conclusions as some meetings might. But that conference was attended by all the premiers of Canada, many of the governors of the various provinces and also by representatives of the Dominion Government. The question of furnishing assistance for roads was one of the questions which was discussed and it was a question that was put forward by the representatives of the provinces as one of the methods by which we might tide over the reconstruction period. At that time we were discussing it from an entirely nonpolitical standpoint. I had never seen the time when men representing all shades of political thought in Canada got together, or sat around a table and discussed how best we could work together to get out of this difficulty than I saw on that occasion. We discussed a dozen different things and among them the question of assistance to highways. Some of the premiers stated that they could not agree to any policy by which the Dominion would invade the provinces and take possession of their roads. I think they were quite right in that. All the provinces were anxious that the Dominion should pass some sort of legislation by which they could assist in the construction of highway roads. This Bill was brought down. It was mentioned in the speech from the Throne, and it was brought down very largely as a result of the conference to which , I have referred.
As to the question of the value of highway roads, I am not going to take up any time over that, because I am talking to gentlemen every one of whom knows the value of highway roads as well as I do. Some hon. members say that you will not employ labour in the country. I do not agree with that at all. We are all too prone to argue these things from the conditions existing in Winnipeg, Toronto, and, perhaps, Montreal. They are important parts of Canada, but they are not the whole of Canada by any means. In my judgment they are a very small part of Canada. It is not a question of whether you have 10,000 or 20,000 men in the city of Toronto who are out of work, but who will not go out into the country and seek it. It is a question of what-we are going to do with the great body of labouring people in this country in the rural district small towns and villages and most of us represent that class of the community. We have hundreds and thousands of men in these small towns, villages and rural constituencies who want to work and who do not want ten hours' pay for a six-hour day, but who want

to give ten hours of labour and get ten hours' pay for it. We have people who are willing to work ahd this is the class of people who would be employed if this work goes on. The construction of good macadamized, but not concreted, permanent or semi-permanent roads through the country produces the greatest asset that it is possible to have. It is not a question of a man drawing his grain to market. That is a very small part of it in my judgment. It is a matter of dollars and cents as to how much it is going to cost a man to get the produce of the farm marketed, but away above and beyond that is the great part that good roads play in making the people contented. If this country is ever going to get out .of its financial troubles, if this country is ever to be made the home of a happy, contented people, if it is going to keep the people in the country districts, villages, and small towns happy and contented, it must give them goqd highway roads. Give the people of any community good highway roads that they can travel pver and use, give them telephone communication with the cities, towns and villages and you will have a happy and contented people. I know of no way in which .you can expend a sum of money in order .to get this country on its feet again, to get .ahead and to make ourselves believe that we are not bankrupt than in the way that is proposed in this measure. Nothing can .conduce to that happy condition of affairs more than by helping towards the construction of highway roads. I believe that my attitude on this question is absolutely consistent with the ground that I have taken on the question of economy in this House and I am going to take the consequences. I believed then that it was the ground, I believe it now and if this becomes law I am sure that nothing that has been done by this Government will do more to bring about peace and harmony and get us back to normal conditions than will be done by the adoption of this Bill the purpose of which is to provide for a better transportation system.
, Mr. DAVIDSON: If the Minister of Public Works is consistent and in favour of this principle, may I ask him why he did not support the legislation for good roads as it was introduced under the Good Roads Act of 1913-13?

That is six years ago
and I have too much to do to look up the debates of that time. But my memory is pretty good and unless I am very much 
mistaken I supported exactly the principle which I am advocating to-day, although it is six years ago, I opposed a Bill which meant that the Federal Government went into a province and built highways. I think that if my hon. friend will look up the statement which I made at that time he will find that I said that under clause 6-
I think it was-the Minister of Railways could go into my constituency and build a highway or a culvert. I opposed that part of the Bill. I did vote, however, for a federal grant so long as it was handed pver to the provinces, without invading their rights in any way, and that they had the handling of the money. I stand on that ground to-day.

A long time has elapsed since, then and I have not in the interval read the Senate amendment, but I know what I stood for in the House of Commons:
I stood for the granting of federal aid to [DOT] highways, so long as the money was expended by the provinces and not by the Dominion.
This is a different proposition. This proposes expenditure and operation by interlocking and double machinery.
No, I cannot agree with my hon. friend at all.
Question.

I have very little to say on this question. Like the Minister of Public Works, I was in the House when, the subject came up in 1912. I then took exactly the same position as did the Minister of Public Works of the present day. We were willing to give aid for building roads in this country provided the money was expended under the control of the provinces.
I stand in the same place now. There is this difference between the former policy and the. present one, as I understand it, that this expenditure is, to all intents and purposes, to be under the cohtrol of the different provinces. If the question were coming up to-day for the first time, without any preliminary arrangements having been entered into, and everybody having a free hand, I am not going to say, in view of the financial conditions of the country, what attitude I would take. But I do not feel

that conditions which have developed for some montihs past can very easily, and without consideration, he set aside. In the views which I express, I am speaking largely for the province- from which I come. I know that some time last December the Premier of Nova Scotia, with other premiers, met in a conference in this city and a certain policy in respect to aiding the construction of roads was agreed upon. The Federal Government announced in the speech from the Throne last February what its policy, was, and that it was going to implement that policy by bringing down a Bill. I am in a position to know that the Government of Nova Sco'tia, acting upon the arrangement or agreement entered into, made provision for the meeting of the stipulated conditions by putting itself in a position to furnish tihe sixty cents for every forty cents that is to be expended Iby the Federal Government. Now being aware that the Premier of Nova Scotia and his government are to-day waiting to carry out the fulfilment of the arrangement referred to; knowing the mind of the Premier of Nova Scotia on the point and what he has said to me about it; knowing that the people of the province are agreeable to this policy and to this scheme, and that they are awaiting the carrying out of the whole programme as a result of the action of this House; knowing what has already been done by the local legislature and what will be done by the Government, I would not feel justified at this stage in obstructing in any way a policy which I think is approved of by the people of my province and by the Government of the Hon. Mr. Murray. For these reasons if a vote is taken I shall vote in support of the Bill.
Question.

I will occupy only a very brief period of time; I merely rise for the purpose of speaking in favour of the proposition. I shall not have the pleasure of voting for it, if a vote takes place, because I am paired, but I wish to 'be distinctly understood as supporting this scheme. It is a measure which, in my judgment, is for the general advantage of Canada, and it can be classified under that heading. The improvement of the roads of Canada will bring about, as the Minister of Public Works has very well illustrated, good results. It will produce' good results to the farming community and place them in a much better position than they would otherwise be. In that respect I consider it is a proposition for the general advantage of
the countey, and were I voting I would record my vote in favour of it.

I wish to offer a few observations before this discussion closes about a certain phase of the matter. I am advised that the minister who is in charge of the Bill has intimated that it is brought forward in fulfilment of a pledge made prior to the election of 1917. I did not know of the pledge at the time, but that does not make any difference. I would be the last person in the world to say a word against the fulfilment of pledges, but I would respectfully suggest that priority in, pledges should have priority of fulfilment. I could mention a number of pledges made by members of the present Government, pledges made long before this matter ever came up, which have not yet been carried out in their entirety. I referred to one of these pledges during the Budget debate a short time ago. Prior to 1911 a solemn pledge was made that if the Conservative party were returned to power the national resources of the western provinces would be handed over to those provinces. This pledge has not yet been carried out, and there is no intimation that it is likely to be fulfilled at an early date.
I also wish to mention the matter of the Hudson Bay railway. In 1896, Sir Charles Tupper, then the head of the Conservative party, promised if his party were returned to power the construction of the Hudson Bay railway would be immediately undertaken and brought to a conclusion at an early date. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Mr. Laurier, made a similar promise. The latter was returned to office, and somewhat late in the history of his administration I admit, along toward the end of the Liberal term of office, the construction of the Hudson Bay railway was begun.. If I remember correctly, the right hon. gentleman who now leads the Government also promised at certain times that if he were returned to power he would see that the Hudson Bay railway was taken up and carried to completion as soon as possible-in fact I do not know of any public undertaking in the whole of the Dominion that was so universally supported as the Hudson Bay project.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is not discussing the Bill.
Yes, I am.

I think the hon. gentleman is wandering rather far afield in his argument, and I

would therefore ask him to confine himself more closely to the clause under discussion.

I am sure my hon.
friend would not wish to misrepresent anything I said. I did not state that the people of this country had no confidence in the Government. I could not possibly state that, because I do not know the opinions of the people. What I did say was that I had met a great many people who strongly supported Union Government at its formation and at the last election, but who would not subscribe to another domestic loan because they had not confidence, from the way this Government are handling the finances of the country, that they would spend another loan wisely.
That is about the same thing.

I would like to ask the Government how they reconcile their actions with the financial condition of the country at the present time. I understood from the Government that we are something like $100,000,000 short of our carrying charges. I could understand the Government borrowing money to expend on works that were regarded as of a capital nature, for instance, railways or public works that would be expected to return something on the money invested in them, but from what the Government have told us I gather that the country is not able to pay its way. If a private concern were in the position that the Dominion Government say they are in to-day, it would be considered as bankrupt. If the business, was losing money to the extent that it was necessary to borrow fresh money to pay interest on its outstanding obligations, and it was not able to get in enough revenue to pay its rhnning expenses, it would be considered bankrupt. If that is the position of the Dominion Government to-day-.and I think the Finance Minister will agree with me that it is- while we have greater facilities for borrowing, we are in no different position than a private concern would be so far as sound	financing is concerned.	I
[DOT]want to put this question to the Government: Do you hope next year you will be able to collect enough money in taxes to pay the current expenses of the country? If you do, why, you must resort to some heavier form of taxation than the present, and there is no reason why you should not have resorted to it this year,
because if you are going on borrowing to pay for current expenses you will ultimately get deeper in the hole. In the face of that condition, why should you borrow money to give to the provinces when they are not asking for it? There was the argument in 1912 that you had a full treasury,-thanks to the good administration of the Liberal party which left you in that position the previous year. But that is not the state of affairs to-day. You have no money to give away, you must go out in the market and borrow not only the money you propose to give to the provinces for this work,' but the money to meet the ordinary running expenses of the country, and you must add interest on top of the money you are borrowing.
You are borrowing money and paying interest and must continue to borrow in order to pay interest on the interest. Naturally, therefore, we are facing serious conditions' in this country. Of course, while we are spending money lavishly there is apparent prosperity; money is flowing freely and values are inflated. But there must be a time of settlement, and surely it is not good business for the Government to continue to pile up this debt and increase the obligation which the people must eventually settle.
The argument is used that this work would be advantageous in that it would find employment for returned soldiers. Six months ago, or a year ago, that might have looked like good business; it appeared to be necessary to take steps to find employment for the soldiers when they returned. But apparently that is not the condition to-day. I am told by farmers that they have great difficulty in finding farm help. As several members have pointed out, the labour that will be employed on these roads will be the kind of labour that would otherwise be employed on the farm. There is no question about the value of good road's. Everybody is agreed as to that, but as I pointed out a few days ago, the people of my constituency want the good roads there, if they are to pay for them; they do not want good roads to be built in some other constituency at their expense. I am sure that the same feeling prevails in many other constituencies. In my constituency we are trying to get good roads and we are trying to build them with our own money and to pay for the work, as far as possible, as we go along. But the conditions under which this money is being handed over are not such as to enable any municipality or any district in a given province to get a portion of the money if they
Let them build them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Give the people of Quebec and Ontario and of the other provinces of this country good roads, and you immediately increase the profits of the farmer, even if he sells his products at the same price, because the cost of haulage would be so much less. There are farmers in the Canadian Northwest, thousands of them, twenty miles and more from a railway. With the roads as they are, the haulage of a load of wheat twenty miles to the elevator will amount to 10 cents a bushel. If the farmer can haul twice as much over a better road you have reduced the price to 5 cents a bushel. There is no policy that the governments of this country, provincial and Dominion, can carry into effect of more national benefit to the people of Canada than the improvement of highways. The citizen who is immediately benefited is the farmer, but he is not the only one benefited. Good roads, as the Minister of Public Works has pointed out, will make farming more agreeable; it will make life on the farm more comfortable and enable the farmer to get much-needed recreation, and in that way it will relieve the monotony of his life upon the farm. If there is one thing this country needs to-day more than another it is a policy that will make life upon the farm more attractive, in order that those now on the farm may be contented, and that the sons of those now on the farm may, if they have a liking for farming, remain upon the farm, and that others may be attracted to it.
So far as the general question is concerned, there is no policy that should appeal more to the farmers of this country than a policy respecting the improvement of highways. Towns and cities immediately dependent upon the country will also be benefited, and so it goes all the way up the line. Whatever you do to improve agricul-



ture and benefit the farmer inures to the benefit and advantage of the whole of Canada.
So say we all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, you do, but you don't vote that way.
We build our own roads in Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will see how you vote on this. If you want to help the farmer, support this Bill. My hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) speaks for the province of Quebec. He is a representative and able man, but I submit that he is no more representative and no more able than the Premier of the province of Quebec.
They are not acting in the same capacity. We represent the whole Dominion in this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Dominion Government is interested in the welfare of every part of the Dominion. Last December we called a provincial conference here. It was a proper thing to do. All these Provincial Governments are properly interested in the development of their provinces, and the question before us was the question of re-construction. It was a live question then, and it would be more live to-day but for what the Government has done. No Government ever gets credit for what it prevents. Look at the situation in this country to-day, the best in the world, I believe, outside of the United States, and I am not sure that it is not better than that of the United States. Instead of giving the Government credit for what has been done, and for what we have prevented, it is all taken for granted and we are criticised because we expend money. Why, it has been the expenditure of money that has kept us going. I do not mean to say that it can continue indefinitely, but I do say that until demobilization is complete and the immediate consequences of this war are over, this Government would be derelict in its duty if it did not have the courage to take the measures necessary to keep the people of this country employed so far as we can. They have suffered much, and the country owes them a great deal.
Coming more immediately to the question of provincial jurisdiction, local works, under the British North America Act, are under the jurisdiction of the province. But is there anything to hinder the provinces coming to us, as they have done since 1910, and asking us to increase their subsidies? There

is no hon. gentleman who will say that the Dominion Government would not be within its jurisdiction in increasing the subsidies to the several provinces. What are we proposing to do? We are not taking away from the Provincial Governments of this country the control of their roads or the administration of this work. What we are doing, by giving them what is virtually a subsidy, is enabling them to carry on road building on a scale that they could not and would not do otherwise. That is the point. It is idle to say that the provinces have the credit and will do this work themselves. The provinces will do nothing of the kind. If the Dominion Government does not assist the provinces by these subsidies, because, practically they are subsidies to the provinces, it means that this country will not have the good roads; that is all.
* Some hon. MEMBERS: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. Some hon. gentlemen have said that Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have floated loans at a certain rate; but how big a loan? A province can put out a loan of $1,000 000 or $2,000,000, but hon. gentlemen know that they could not float a loan of $25,000,000 or $50,000,000 or $100,000,000. The volume of your borrowing has to be taken into account. It is one of the most important things.
The $20,000,000 would not have to be raised by one province but would be divided among nine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not stating that any one province would have to raise $20,000,000. I simply used the illustration of $25,000,000, $50,000,000 and $100,000,000 to show that it did not necessarily follow that because a province could raise a million or two they could raise five or ten million or more. I say this and I know it from talking with the provincial treasurers and with the premiers of the several provinces. I know perfectly well that if the Dominion Government does not assist them in the way we are now proposing by subsidizing road building in the provinces, those roads will not be built; that is all. The provinces will build to a certain extent undoubtedly.
Mr. MoCREA:	Quebec has spent over
$20,000,000 on roads and is spending more than she will receive under this scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Quebec is a great province, but it is not the only one. Quebec and many other provinces will not do anything like the amount of road building that will be accomplished if this legislation goes through. We know what we are

talking about because we have been in consultation with the prime ministers and treasurers of these various provinces. I am aware of their financial position, and what the Minister of Public Works has stated is correct. They are pressed financially because we have invaded the field from which they would ordinarily derive revenues, and they have very many expenditures upon them which have greatly increased during the war. Hon. members say that soldiers will not work on the roads. Let us assume that that is so. One would think that one part of the industry of the country was in no way related to another. The business of the country as a whole is built up upon the basic industries connected with our natural resources. Will any hon. gentleman say that if we have a large road building programme being carried out all over Canada, employing hundreds and thousands of men, the results of that expenditure will not be felt in the villages and towns and cities? Will not the soldiers and others in those places who are not immediately engaged in road building have the benefit of the re-active effect upon business derived from that road building and founded upon it, and the expenditure oi money that will take place? I am the last man to say that a nation should attempt to lift itself by its boot straps, but I am profoundly interested in this question: What is going to happen in the country next year? What about next winter? Hon. gentlemen, including the hon. member for Red Deer, criticised the better housing scheme. Yet this Industrial Cbmmission that brings down its report is in favour of better housing. The provinces could not raise the money for that purpose and the Dominion lends it to them, and if that money is wisely expended in building houses 'and providing the material for them, it is going to go a long way to relieve unemployment during next winter, which will be a critical winter. This fall, if this legislation goes through, they will get Teady and proceed with the work to a certain extent and employment will be provided for men in the towns and villages and the countrysides, and this will keep families from distress. If we do not pass this legislation they will not go ahead with the work in the provinces. The leader of the Opposition himself indicated how important it is to the province of Nova Scotia. Premier Murray at the Provincial Conference said that years ago he used to consider carefully whether a matter was within provincial or Dominion jurisdiction, and as to whether the province would be justi-2804
fled in accepting a grant from the Dominion with respect to something that did . not appear to be in the letter of the constitution. But, he said, he had got over that; and he is a wise man. He said that it is a question of what is best in the interests of Nova Scotia, and if the Dominion Government can assist them in a better roads programme that would furnish employment there, improve agriculture in Nova Scotia, and have its general beneficial effect on the business of the province, he is in favour of it. These are the general considerations upon which ihe Government have reached the conclusion that we should assist the provinces in improving the highways in this country.
Another aspect of the question I may touch upon. I have spoken to-day only from the domestic standpoint, but this country should be a great pleasure resort, so to speak, for the people of the south, and there is nothing that will bring tourists here and bring a circulation of money on a scale we do not realize, more than the improvement of our highways. Consider the development of the motor within the last ten or fifteen years. There are thousands of them in every section of the country, and the tourist is not to be disregarded. In Europe a great deal of importance is attached to the tourist traffic because it brings so much money to the country. Now, Sir, you can brush aside the matter of constitutionality, for the question resolves itself into this: Having regard to the fact that we are practically in a war period-the re-construction period following war, and having regard to the possibilities of unemployment on a great scale during the coming year and the fact that this legislation will very largely assist the agriculture of the provinces and promote business generally, the question is whether the Dominion Government is justified in raising money for the purposes of assisting the provinces in this matter. If we reach the conclusion in this House that the Government would have been justified in November last in shutting down and taking the position that we would not spend another dollar and would let things go, then the House should deny the vote. But if, on the other hand, this House intends to be constructive in this period, as I believe the people of Canada require them to be, then, in regard to a vote such as this for productive purposes' that will give employment to the people who have suffered greatly during the war, and prevent distress on a wide scale, it should sup-

port the Government in the proposal it has brought down.
Mr. Chairman-
Question.

Just one word-
Some hon. MEMBERS': Question.
Go on.

We are in committee
land it happens to be a rule of the House of Commons, probably not familiar to some hon. members, that in committee we may speak as often as we are fortunate enough to get the opportunity. There is no hurry; (we are in fine weather. However, I shall only keep the committee for a moment, iwdth a benevolent purpose in view. My right honourable friend the Prime Minister must, I am sure, be impressed with the extraordinary facility of speech which his Minister of Finance has developed during his prolonged absence. His facility of finance and expression is so great that my hon. friend really appears to deceive himself. He gives you many figures'-500,000 returned soldiers, the number of people who have gone into employment who were previously out of employment, and so on, and sums the situation up with the facility and dexterity of a conversational conjurer, concluding with the question:	" If
we had shut everything down what would have happened in the country?" He has improved a little in recent years in regard to the use of the personal pronoun. He does not say:	" If I had shut down," but
" if we had shut down." Now the delusion I want to remove from my hon. friend's mind is this. He is under the impression that every returned soldier who has gone back to work has been provided with that employment by his extraordinary management of the finances of the country and Jais absolute carelessness as to the amount of money he borrows., I want him to dwell upon the fact that from the Atlantic to the Pacific, in this very large country, the farmers' sons in every province and in every district of every province have returned from the war ;by the facilities afforded by the Government and have been only too glad to get back to their homes on the farms and enter into the operation of those farms, without the minister having had anything whatever to do with it, except in so far as the (Government has provided the means of transportation. In every city in this coun-

try, from coast to coast, large employers of labour have been busying themselves from the middle of the war, the very moment when our men began to come back, in getting employment in their works for their men who had gone overseas. They have been placing those men 'back at work and have not been borrowing money to spend on roads in order to do it. In every village in the country the same thing has been going on, and I want my friend to be reasonable in the claims he makes upon the support and regard of this country, because I venture to say to him, with respect to the men who have gone back to work, that his borrowing schemes, his shipbuilding schemes, his housing schemes and his road-making schemes have had no more to do with the matter than the man in the moon.

I have listened with considerable interest during the entire day and on previous occasions to the debate on this subject. I had also the privilege in 1912 and 1913 to be a member of this'House when a similar discussion took plaoe. Perhaps it will not be amiss to recall that discussion so that new members may realize something of the history of this legislation and perhaps, in passing that history under review, be enabled to reach a conclusion this afternoon as to how they should vote. It is my intention particularly to direct the attention of the House to the constitutional aspect of the question because the hon. member from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark), with characteristic energy and force, has placed that side of. the argument in the forefront. In 1912, if my memory serves me correctly, the question of highway assistance was first introduced in this House. The principle that underlay that measure was that the Dominion Government should supply the money and should undertake the construction of the Toa'ds themselves when approved. When that measure went to the Senate for concurrence, concurrence was denied on the ground that it was an interference with provincial rights and that if the Dominion Government granted assistance towards the construction of highways it should 'be by direct vote to the provinces and not by undertaking the work themselves. The result was that in 1912 the legislation became of no effect due to the fact that the concurrence of the Senate could not be obtained.
In 1913 the subject was again brought before the House of Commons for consideration, and I should like to read to

the House one section of the Bill because it casts considerable light on the constitutional question. If any hon. gentleman has in his hand Bill No. 152, that we are now considering, and will be good enough to read paragraph (a) at the top of page 2 he will see the remarkable similarity between what was section 4 of 'the Act of 1913 and section 2 of the present Bill. Section 4 of the Bill of 1913 reads as follows:
Any highway or bridge for which aid is granted to a province shall toe improved or constructed, as the case may be, according to descriptions, conditions land specifications approved toy the Governor in Council and on the report of the minister, and' specified in each case in an agreement between the minister and the government of the province, which agreement the minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council, is hereby empowered to make.
That laid down the principle, as between the Dominion and the province, that the Senate did not object to there being an agreement provided 'the money was spent by the province. In sustaining my position, let me read what Senator Beique said, page 622-3 of the Senate Hansard, 1913:
I am not aware that a single member of this hon. House quarrels with this fourth clause of the 'Bill. It is worded as it was amended by this House last year, and It was approved toy. the House of Commons, and I take It that we are unanimous in favour of that section.
When the House of Commons objected to the reception of 'the Senate amendment by which the money was to be paid to the province, a message was sent back to the Senate insisting that the money must be spent by the Dominion Government. In reply to that message the Senate sent hack the following message:
That the Senate adheres to the seventh amendment for the following among other reasons-
The seventh amendment being that the money should be spent 'by the provinces:
1.	Because section 6 of the Bill empowers the minister to undertake the construction or improvement of highways in any province, which would be a contravention of the letter and spirit of the British North America Act, 1867, and of the uniform practice under that Act, for which contravention no sufficient cause has been shown.
2.	Because the said amendment affirms in effect that it is undesirable that the minister or the Dominion Government should usurp the functions of the provincial administration in the building and maintenance of highways and bridges.
And I would particularly direct the attention of the House to what I am now reading:
3.	Because the said amendment will not hamper the administration in carrying out its policy in supplying the funds placed in the Estimates for that object under conditions and regulations it may deem just and1 proper to make, sufficient provision being made in earlier clauses of the Bill for co-operation between the Federal and provincial governments.
What does that mean? It means that the Senate, in 1913, and the Liberal Opposition of that day, accepted the principle that, provided the money was paid to the province to be expended by the province, it would not be unconstitutional and 'that an arrangement should be made as to the method of construction as to specifications and descriptions of highways provided such au arrangement could be made between the province and the Dominion.
I therefore submit that the hon. member for Red Deer and the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) are inconsistent in contending that what the Government is asking us to do is unconstitutional when they voted for exactly the same thing in 1913. Why do I say thait they voted for exactly the same thing in 1913? In 1913, by clause 4, provision was made for the setting aside of certain highways and the entering into oE certain agreements between the Dominion and the province as to the spending of money. The Senate agreed that that was right and proper and the members of the Opposition accepted that position as against the contention of the Conservative party that the money should be spent by the Dominion. Let us turn for a moment to Bill No. 152, the Bill that is before the Committee this afternoon. Clause 3 points out that a- certain amount of money shall be used for highway purposes and that the payments shall be- made on the " following conditions." What are the following conditions? Clause (a) reads as follows:
Any highway for which aid is granted1 shall be constructed or improved, as the case may be, in accordance with the terms of art agreement to be made by the minister with the government of the province, which agreement shall contain such provisions as to cost, description, specifications or otherwise a-s the Governor in Council may approve;
Exactly the same terms as are set out in section 4 of the Bill of 1913 and for which the hon. member for Red Deer, the hon. member for Three Rivers and other hon. members voted.
There has been no man in this House who has taken a stronger stand in the past few years in favour of economy than has the member for Kingston. But certainly I think this Highway Improvement Act is in a totally different position from a proposal

that means the spending of money for something that is not productive. I stated a few nights ago in this House that I saw various advantages that would result from the improvement of our roadways. One was that it would bring into this country many tourists who would leave a large amount of money in the Dominion and whose coming here I felt would be of great advantage to Canada. But far and beyond that is the improvement that would result to rural life in Canada. I know something-not a great deal because I am an urban rather than a rural resident-of the disadvantages under which the rural population in Ontario live, particularly in the early spring and the late fall. I do know that with the advent of the motor car, which is in very general use now, the farmer enjoys a measure of comfort which was previously denied him. But he is at a great disadvantage in that the full enjoyment of the motor car is not possible to our farming community because our roads are not constructed to carry a motor car over them with the minimum of wear and tear. Our macadam roads are breaking down, a great many have become impossible, and I believe that nothing will contribute more to the improvement of the conditions of life in the rural parts of Ontario than a substantial improvement in our roads.
And, Sir, I am not going to urge that the construction of trunk lines should be the only consideration. It is aboslutely essential that the side line roads should be improved as well as the main thoroughfares. If there is not sufficient money at the present day to improve the main roads how are the Governments of the provinces going to improve the side line roads? But, if this substantial grant proposed under this Bill is made to the provinces, it will relieve them of some of the burden incidental to main line construction and will make further sums of money available for the purpose of side line betterment. On rising I said that I should endeavour to confine myself largely to the constitutional question, and I think I have demonstrated beyond the shadow of a doubt that the constitutional argument, as raised to-day, was brushed aside in 1912 as not worthy of consideration, and that the Bill in the form in which it is drafted this afternoon had the approval of the 'Senate and of the Liberal party who then were His Majesty's loyal Opposition.

The hon. member for Kingston has pronounced hon. members opposite who voted for the Senate amendment in 1913 inconsistent because they do

not support the present measure. Will he tell the House what he thinks of his own consistency in now supporting a proposition which he voted against in 1913?

The hon. member for
Kingston in 1913 wanted the construction of good roads and was prepared to assume the responsibility of those roads being built by the Dominion Government. In the year 1919 the hon. member for Kingston still wants good roads, and if it is impossible to secure legislation by which the Dominion may build them, he is prepared to support legislation that will ensure good roads being built by the provinces.

I have listened with great attention to the speech which has been made by the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat. He has accused the member for Red Deer (Mr. 'Michael Clark) and the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) of being inconsistent. I have listened to The speeches in question, and I do not think the hon. gentlemen who delivered them can be considered inconsistent. On both sides of the House we accept the principle of good roadis; there is not a man in the House who is against the building of good roads in any province of the Dominion. If the Bill only provided for good roads if the Government had the money to build those roads and if the country could do what the Bill contemplates doing, without increasing our indebtedness, which is huge already, there would be no trouble. When the Bill was first introduced, as remarked by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Nickle), the Liberal opposition at the time said they did not want to vote in favour of the measure if the Federal Government proposed to interfere in any way with provincial autonomy. That was the position taken by the Opposition at that time, led by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. But the present Government has improved the good roads measure as originally introduced, and I congratulate it upon having done so. The Government has accepted the attitude taken by the Opposition at the time referred to, and in that respect has made it their own. Provincial autonomy is respected by this Bill and now the only question is, can the Government to-day make, in addition to its already very large outlays, a further expenditure of $25,000,000 for this purpose. We say we do not think the time is proper to do so, and therefore I nan see no inconsistency in the attitude taken by either of the two hon. gentlemen who have been criticised. The Minister of Finance delivered a very elo-

quent speech; the hon. member for Bed. Deer has given an answer which is very fit,
I understand and believe. But I would remind the Minister of Finance of one fact, that the province of Quebec throughout the war has kept down its public undertakings and its public works, and has kept down its financing, and never during that period did it come to beg from the Minister of Finance. That hon. gentleman seems to believe that if it had not been for the Federal Government none of the provinces of Canada could have survived the period of the war. I do not wish to speak for any other province than my own, and I say that the province of Quebec has gone through that period and constructed public works that were imperatively needed, and notwithstanding that fact our financial standing to-day as a province is away above the financial standing of Canada as a Dominion. Moreover, when the provincial treasurer submitted his last budget speech to the Legislative Assembly he could say without being contradicted that there was a surplus for the year of $2,000,000, and more than that, Sir Lomer Gouin's Government, during the war period, has met all its liabilities and its obligations and has hardly borrowed any money.
Now, as regards good roads, the Minister Oif Finance says if the Bill is not passed the provinces will not be in a position to construct these works. I take issue with the minister, and I say that that statement is not in any way in conformity with the facts.
Hear, hear.

In 1912, without the aid of the Federal Government in any way whatsoever, the Government of Quebec inaugurated a good roads system, and what was the result? From the year 1912 to the year 1919 the sum of $12,000,000 was spent by it in that province. I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman, the total expenditure for the purpose was $20,000,000, and the Premier of Quebec is in no way seeking the help of the Federal Government to continue his progressive policy. During the provincial contest recently ended, Sir Lomer Gouin said that not only would he continue his policy of building good roads, but that he would increase it. If the province of Quebec has done that much, why is it the other provinces cannot do the same? My opinion is that they can do just as well. The Western Provinces are not asking for the help of the Federal Government, neither are the Maritime Provinces. I heard the Minister of Finance say that the premiers
of the different provinces came together in a conference in this city and declared they were in favour of this Bill. Mr. Chairman, we have not the official proceedings of that conference before us. During another discussion I heard the President of the Privy Council assert, as regards Dominion aid to agriculture, that the premiers of the different provinces had made declarations to the same effect. It may be so, but I maintain that we, as the representatives of the people are not here to vote for the reckless expenditure of public moneys; we are here to safeguard the rights of the people whom we represent. It is about time that a stop was made to the extravagant expenditure of money in Canada. The Federal Government has expended millions and millions of dollars, and when the members from this side ask the Finance Minister where he is going to get the money for those expenditures, his usual answer is: "We will borrow." We have had enough borrowing in Canada, we do not want any more of it. This is not only the feeling of gentlemen who sit on this side, but similar declarations have been made in another branch of this Parliament, and throughout the country as well. We want those who are governing this country to return to their normal senses. We must not forget, Mr. Chairman, that Canada is a country of but seven millions in population. I heard the Minister of Finance say in respect to England, that it was floating an enormous loan; but, Mr. Chairman, before comparing loans made by the United Kingdom with loans made by Canada, the resources of the two countries should be compared. Is Canada in the same position in point of wealth and resources that England is? We have been imitating England too much in this country. We have forgotten that England is an old country with enormous and unlimited resources, whereas we are only a young country, and the best advice I can give to the Finance Minister is to come off his financial stilts. Let him come right down to the common basis of financing that is adopted in normal times. Let him stop talking about hundreds of millions of dollars, when the total revenue of Canada is only $270,000,000, and when out of that sum we require to take $150,000,000 to pay the interest on our debt and the pensions to our soldiers. That is the situation, and the people are appalled at the way things are being run by the Government. It is about time that they were stopped.

I may say to 'the Minister of Finance, Mr. Chairman, that he is not the first man who has attempted to run a country by these financial means. Let us go hack in history. Let us see, for instance, how Law and Necker ran the finances of France for a while and how the Duke of Choiseuil ran the finances of France for a while. The duke, whenever he needed money, did like the Minister of Finance-he borrowed it. It was always easy to borrow, but it was sometimes very hard to pay back, and when the time of.accounting came the Duke was in this awful financial position: He had borrowed so much money that it was impossible to pay it back. What was the result? The overthrow of the Government and the Revolution, with all the terrible things that happened during that period.
The Minister of Finance says that the farmers want good roads. I am very much surprised to hear of the hon. minister paying such an awful lot of attention to the farmers. Not very long ago he paid very little attention to them, and, when they wanted something more than good roads, he denied it to them. Instead of giving good roads to the farmers, let the hon. minister give them a lower tariff. That would be far better philosophy, and the country would be in a much better position.

The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

One of the weak points in this Bill is that if one of the provinces does not wish to take advantage of its provisions, that province will nevertheless be taxed for expenditures made in other provinces. For instance, if Saskatchewan does not take advantage of this legislation and Ontario does, or Quebec does, a portion of the money spent in Ontario or in Quebec will be paid into the federal treasury by the taxpayers of Saskatchewan. The principle is unsound; the people of one province should not be taxed for works which, under this legislation, are carried on in another province. I said this afternoon that the province of Quebec had already spent on highways the sum of $20,000,000. Is it fair to Quebec that, commencing this year, money should be given by the Federal Government to other provinces which are building highways and that Quebec should get absolutely nothing in respect of the roads which that province has already built? Under this Bill any province which 
spends one dollar on highways is entitled to receive forty cents from the. federal treasury; on that basis Qubbee, in respect of the $20,000,000 already spent, would be entitled to receive $8,000,000 from the federal treasury. Because Quebec was the pioneer in highway building; because Quebec did more than the other provinces did. is Quebec to be placed in an inferior position? If all provinces are to be fairly treated, Quebec should receive something for the work which she has already done.
I heard, with great surprise, the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) say that this Bill had been approved by the electors of Canada in the election of 1917. I do not wish to raise in this Committee the old issues of 1917, but when the President of the Council points to the result of that election as an argument in favour of this Bill, he is using what was used in France to deceive the Germans-camouflage.	The
1917 election was fought on one issue, and on one issue only; that issue is well known to all members of the Committee. There was no question in 1917 of giving moneys to the provinces, especially of giving money to the province from which I come, because any man who at that time proclaimed in Ontario that the Federal Government, if returned to power, would give millions of dollars to Quebec, -would not have been well received on the hustings of Ontario. To add further strength to what I say, may I remind hon. gentlemen of certain declarations that were made by members of the Cabinet at that time? I do not wish to repeat them all; I simply recall what the Solicitor General said in several constituencies of Ontario, when he thanked God that in Australia there was no province of Quebec. During the elections of 1917, therefore, there were certainly no appeals to the electors of Ontario in favour of giving money to Quebec for the construction of highways. Moreover, the Government has certainly no endorsation from the people of this measure.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Car-veil) said that members from the province of Quebec had made many demands upon his department for the building of roads in that province. I do not know what the other members from Quebec on this side of the House did, but so far as I am concerned, I never made any demand upon the minister for the building of roads in my county. The roads in Dorchester have been built by the provincial government, and we are satisfied with the work that has been done. What the minister said

may be right or may be wrong as regards members from other parts of Quebec, but so far as my constituency is concerned, his statement is altogether unfounded in fact.
Mine also.

The Minister of Public Works said that the province of Quebec had asked for money for the Laprairie road, and that the province had obtained several hundred thousand dollars from the Federal treasury for the building of that highway. I have sat in the provincial Legislature, and while there I heard mention of this road, which ever since 1910 has been maintained by the federal Government, and which has always been considered as a federal road. When the federal Government, therefore, gave the province of Quebec money in respect of this road, they were only continuing a course which they had been following for nine years, ever since 1910. I do not wish to be misunderstood, we in the province of Quebec are as much in favour of good roads as anybody else in this country.

Allied countries, perhaps we could afford to spend millions; hut the Prime Minister has 'been bach a month now, and he has not had one word to say in this House in regard to tihe Peace Conference, although he was over there six months. I infer from his silence that we are not going [DOT] to get one dollar. Therefore, we ought to have very strict economy in this country, and the stricter the economy the better satisfied will our people be. One last word.
Hear, (hear.

I am quite sure these gentlemen are pleased I am going to finish my speech, but I warn hon. gentlemen who say " Hear, hear," that when they get home they will find the people saying just what I have said here to-night. According to the Minister of Finance, another Victory Loan is to be floated in this country very soon. When the last Victory Loan was floated the Minister of Finance appealed to the members of this House to help the Government to obtain as much money as possible from the people of Canada. I, like all the other hon. members from the province of Quebec, did my best to promote the Victory Loan, and I think the results obtained in my constituency were very satisfactory. But if the next Victory Loan is to be a success, this Government, as my hon. friend (Mr. Clark) has said, will have to be very careful. People certainly will not give money to the Government unless they feel assured that it is not going to be squandered, but spent as it should be spent. We received $700,000,000 from our last Victory Loan; I do not know what the Minister of Finance will ask for next fall, but if he wishes to make it a success, and it is important that it should be a success, the policy of this Government should be one of prudence. Otherwise, the Victory Loan will be a failure. I do not think this Government intends curtailing expenditure. They wish now to spend $20,000,000. We have done our best to show that this expenditure should not be made at present, so .whether the Bill passes or not we on this side of the House will have the satisfaction of having performed what we thought was our duty to the people of this country.

I would emphasize the remarks made by my hon. friend from Red Deer with regard to the effectiveness of the argument put forward this afternoon by the Minister of Finance, who contended that if this money were not voted the provinces could not and would not build their roads. The minister went on to show what a good thing it was for the Dominion Government to help all the provinces build these roads, and said that the provinces would not do the work without assistance. That is the greatest fallacy that has- ever been advanced heTe. The provinces can and will build roads irrespective of any aid which may be given by the Federal Government. I shall not answer the arguments of the minister, because I think they were very well met by the member for Red Deer, but I would ask the Minister of Railways a question, to which I desire an answer. How are you going to pay the $80,000 each year to the government of each province?

The Bill provides that $80,000 shall be set aside to the credit of each province, and then the amount left will be divided up in proportion to population according to the last federal census. That is done in order to give the smaller provinces a fair portion. We put up forty per cent and they put up sixty per cent when it is agreed to do any work. Now, perhaps I might refer to some of the remarks made by one or two other gentlemen. In the first place, the hon. member for Edmonton-
Before the minister proceeds, does he consider that an answer to my question?
Perhaps I have not answered the hon. member very fully.
Go on. I do not consider that you have.

With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Mackie), the Government feel that in connection with any amount of money advanced we should see that we get full value, and for that purpose the Bill provides, in clause 5, that the Governor in Council may make such regulations as are necessary for giving effect to the objects and purposes of the Act. With regard to the other point, as to the agreement that must be made between the minister and the provincial government, that is for the purpose of keeping supervision over any road that may be built, and of seeing that in the matter of lo,cation the road is laid out in such a way as to ensure that the money will be expended to the best possible advantage and in the best interests of the public.

The paragraph I
read a moment ago distinctly says what the agreement shall be, and I would like to know the meaning of the word " otherwise."

It might have reference to just what I stated-as regards location, for instance. However, if the Committee feels that this clause is not wide enough I have no objections to an amendment. I am not wedded to the wording of the clause as it is now, if anything better can be suggested.

The work can be
done otherwise than by tender.

Possibly there might be some road on which the work could not be done by tender but would have to be done otherwise. But the Government, in view of the feeling that the Committee believes that the work should be done by tender, would in every case endeavour to carry out that policy. If you put that provision in the Bill, however, a case might arise where it would be necessary and advisable, if tenders were considered too high, for the Dominion and local governments to come to an agreement to do the work on force account or by days' labour temporarily, under the supervision of engineers of the Dominion and of the local governments to see that it was done properly and economically pending such time as tenders might be received. Some hon. gentleman suggested that we should provide that the work should be done under the supervision and subject to the approval of an engineer or other officer appointed by the Governor in Coun-

oil. I have no objection to anything of that kind. This Bill originated this year at the Interprovincial Conference, and it was thought at that time that it would provide work for the returned soldiers. Do you intend to build roads in winter time?

Well, the best time in the year to get out the stone required for good roads is in the winter. I am informed that it is necessary to have a very large quantity of stone for the purpose of drainage in connection with the roads.
If it is required to be crushed, it has to be drawn out and crushed in the winter or in the spring. Therefore, any expenditure on good roads will be largely spent in wages. Some hon, members from the province of Quebec have been telling us what has been done in tha't province. There is no doubt that they have done good work in the province of Quebec but they require more good roads, and I believe they will proceed with their construction if this Bill goes through. They wish to proceed with the construction of good roads at a faster pace than in the past. I believe that if this Bill goes through it will be of great service to the unemployed, or those who may be unemployed during next winter. This is not only .for the returned soldiers; there are many men who are being employed at the present time upon railway construction and other works but who next winter will be out of employment. The amount that would be expended would not exceed $4,000,000 per annum. There would not li'ke-

This proposed grant in aid of highways not being class legislation or political in its character, it seems to me that the benefit of it would be enjoyed by all classes. Road improvement will do much towards settling the unrest now prevailing throughout Canada. A fair sharing of the cost by the federal, provincial and municipal authorities will permit the carrying out of well considered legislation and comprehensive plans for road building and maintenance by the provinces and municipalities. We have heard a great deal, and we have boasted considerably, about what the province of Quebec has done in the matter of road building. True, we ought to be proud; Quebec has 2,500 miles of improved road. '	.
The province of Quebec has spent $20,000,000 already, but the demand for good roads is growing and further assistance is desirable, it seems to me. Reference has been made to the possibility of politics intervening in this matter and of influence being exerted to secure the construction of particular pieces of road in .a certain municipality or a certain county. Doubtless efforts may be made in that direction, but according to sub-paragraph (a) of section 4:
Any highway for which aid is granted- shall be constructed or improved, as the case may be, in accordance with the terms of an agreement to be made by the minister with the government of the province, which agreement shall contain such provisions as to costs, descriptions, specifications or otherwise as the Governor in Council may approve.
For my part, I do not see why some hon. members from the province of Quebec are opposed to this Bill. In the paragraph I have quoted there is a guarantee, and in accordance with its terms an agreement must be made by the Federal minister with the Provincial Government. I am going to resume my seat by asking this question: " Have not our friends from the province of Quebec faith in our great and progressive premier, Sir Lomer Gouin"? I am not afraid to depend upon him in preference to any member of this Government. Let this legislation pass, and the agreement arrived at with the province of Quebec will be such as to please the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), the hon. member for .Kamouraska (Mr. E. Lapointe), or any other hon. gentleman who opposes it.

I want to know before I cast my vote-because iny desire is to support this Bill-whether the intention is to construct a trunk road through the country or

to let the money go to the different provinces for the construction of county or other roads?

There is no intention on the part of the Government to insist that this money shall go to the construction of a trunk road extending from one end of the Dominion to the other. The intention is that we shall consult with the Provincial Governments as to what they propose to do. They will submit their plans to us as to where roads in the interest of each province should be looated. The representatives of the Dominion Government will look over those plans, and there will be an agreement as to the particular roads upon which the Federal appropriation would be expended. It would not be fair to insist that all this money shall be devoted to the construction of one trunk line; the expenditure will be distributed through the provinces in the best interests of all concerned and not for the advantage of particular localities in a province as: it would be if we insisted upon the building of a trunk line. What we wish to ensure is that the money shall be expended in the best interests of the people in the province concerned. If we agree to the construction of a particular road, an engineer will be placed on the work to see that the contract is carried out and the money honestly expended and in the best interests of the public. If our engineers report that the contractor is not carrying out his work honestly and ' doing it in the best interests of the community, the attention of the Provincial Government will be drawn to the fact. If, as a result of that, no changes followed, we need not continue paying the money provided for in this Bill. In my opinion the Bill protects the provinces as well as the Dominion, and we will all be able to work together harmoniously. There is no desire except to make the expenditure in the public interest, and I believe that no province in Canada, bearing in mind especially the possibility of unemployment, but will be glad when next winter or summer comes, that they can take advantage of the provisions of this Bill.
If my hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Best) understands the reply of the minister, would he kindly explain it to the committee?
