There is nothing in the Bill which affords information on any of these points, but when we are asked to vote money for this purpose ,we ought to know exactly to what extent the Government is likely to go. I am willing to trust the Prime Minister of Quebec, as my hon. friend from St. James division of Montreal (Mr. L. A. Lapointe) said, but at the same time I am not here as the servant of that Prime Minister. iWhile I am here as the representative of the constituency of Three Rivers, I repre-

sent the whole of Canada and I have to pay regard to the interests of the entire people.
I am not so provincial that I am going to shut my eyes to anything in order to get a few dollars for the province of Quebec if I do not get them fairly. I am not here to praise or criticise one province or the other, but if we are going to pass legislation, let us know what we are passing. There is not a word said, in spite of the explanation given by the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) as to how the money will be paid out. He said, " The money will be paid by cheque." What a childish answer. The money will be paid by cheque! Who does not know that? We know that on payment money has got to change hands.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What did the hon. gentleman mean?

When the Government is going to pay $20 000,000, and a man asks how it is going to be paid, he who answers as the responsible head of the Government ought to know that the question means: Under what terms and conditions and at what times are you going to pay the money. If my right hon. friend does not give me credit for intelligence enough to know that he is going to pay the money by handing it over to whoever is to receive it, one of us has got to be pitied- and I do not pity myself at all in this game. What I want to know is: Under what conditions are you going to pay the money? If the Chairman will permit me I will go to the other section and discuss it. Section 3 says that the money shall be paid as follows:
For the purpose of constructing and improving highways in Canada the 'Governor in Council may authorize the payment out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada of the sum of twenty million dollars during the period of five years from the first day of April, one thousand, nine hundred and nineteen.
Subject to the conditions hereinafter mentioned.
What are the conditions?
Any highway for which aid is granted shall be obstructed or improved, as the case may be, in accordance with the terms of an agreement to be made by ithe minister with the government of the province, which agreement shall contain such provisions as to cost, description, specifications or otherwise as the Governor in Council may approve.
That is as to location, I suppose. We ought to know what standard of road the Government are going to require from the province, anyway, if we are going to agree to that. As I said, they may make any agreement they please; there is no uniformity as to that. They may make one agreement with
the province of Alberta; tney may make another agreement with the province of Saskatchewan; and they may make still another agreement with the province of Manitoba. In spite of the confidence of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in me borrowing possibilities of this country, we want to know what we are doing when we pass this Bill, we want more information. What kind of roads are we going to build? This is a matter we are entitled to know.

Will the hon. gentleman permit me a question? Does he think the provincial authorities would waste their sixty per cent for the purpose of wasting the Dominion's forty per cent on some roads that were worthless?
Where is the provision in the Bill that says the money shall be paid when they have wasted sixty per cent?
That is not an answer.

Where is there anything in the Bill that says that? The other day when we passed a Bill to grant aid to technical education, we said that when the amount shall have been expended
9 p.m. by the province for technical education the Dominion Government will refund it to the province. But here you can make any agreement you please. If the province does not like the agreement it does not enter into it; if it does not enter into it it does not get the money; and if it does not get the money it pays taxes for the good of the provinces that enter into the agreement and get the money. There is the difference. Then you say that the aid so given shall be forty per cent, but there is nothing as to how you are going to give it. You are giving aid under conditions that the House knows nothing about. It is very easy to' say that this money is to be paid for roads which are standardized in the various provinces. We know that the provinces have adopted good roads policies. They know what they ' are about, and it is easy to ascertain what standard of roads they want to have and to grade them. But no, we are called upon to vote $20,000,000, to be expended under an agreement with the Minister of Railways and the provinces, and if any province does not make an agreement it does not get any money. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways was describing just now the work that can be done in the winter time in regard to crushed stone. I do not know how they build roads where he lives, but let me tell my hon. friend that in our province the stone is crushed at the quarry and teamed

or taken by railway to certain parts and spread along the roads as they are built. They do not pay twice for transporting the stone by making dumps and then carting it to the point where it is needed. I see my hon. friends from the Prairie Provinces, and I imagine they would have a long way to haul their stone or gravel for their roads, and it might take them a week or a month in some cases. I see my hon. friends from Winnipeg. How far would they have to go from Winnipeg to load stone? I guess the closest point would be Stony mountain, and in the winter they would hardly make a trip in two days. That argument does not stand. But if I may believe the rumours I hear in the corridors, although the other ministers may be acting in good faith when they say they want to help the soldiers and remove the unrest by having a few loads of stone hauled in the country where probably a road will not be built, the object of this Bill is to permit my hon. friend-I do not blame him, but I am not ready to say I would do the same if I were in his place- to redeem a pledge he made for election purposes that he would see that forty per cent of the cost of a first-class highway between Prescott and Ottawa would be paid by the Government. I do not know whether that is so or not. I see him smile, hut it is the smile of assent, I take it. I do not want to be in his way, and if I knew that to be the case I would be inclined to let the whole thing go through. I have no grudge against the hon. minister, and I admire the way he likes to make his election pledges good even at the expense of the Dominion.

The hon. member states that in the province of Quebec stone is crushed at the quarry. At any place where I have seen good roads under construction a large quantity of ground stone is thrown in to widen the old road, and crushed stone is then drawn for the top dressing. I am not finding fault with the hon. member making the statement about my trying to get this Bill through on account of some election pledge, but let me say that this Bill originated at the meeting of the provincial premiers last fall. It was at their solicitation that we proceeded with the policy of encouraging the construction of good roads. So far as the province of Quebec is concerned, either the deputy or minister or the commissioner of Good Roads interviewed me several times with reference to proceeding with this Bill, and assured me that the provincial government was very anxious that we should go ahead with it. It was brought before the committee, and I

discussed the matter with Sir Lomer Gouin when he was in Ottawa some months ago, but only for a few minutes.
I was certainly under the impression that he was satisfied that this Bill should go through. Perhaps he is not satisfied with the clauses as they now stand in the Bill, but I have never had any complaints from him so far as I can remember. After all, there will be no serious difficulty in making satisfactory arrangements with the provinces as to what roads the money shall be expended upon.
The1 hon. gentleman (Mr. Bureau) asks why we do not lay down specifications showing the kind of roads that the Dominion Government intend to insist upon. But it would be impossible to submit specifications that all the provinces could agree to. One province might want to build a permanent road costing $10,000 a mile; another province-say, Alberta or Saskatchewan-might want to spend the money on a number of roads which would not cost anything like $10,000 a mile. So that it would not be practicable to say that the money shoo US be. spent on roads costing $7,000, $8,000 or $10,000 a mile. The farmers of Alberta and Saskatchewan would,,t in my opinion, receive greater benefit from road-building if roads were built which, though costing very much less, perhaps, than those built in Ontario or Quebec, would be suitable for all their purposes for .many years.
My hon. friend does no1! answer my suggestion with regard to standardization. A standard for each province might be agreed upon.

We could hardly have one standard for Ontario, another for Saskatchewan, 'and so on. The people of New Ontario might want to build roads through country which is being opened up, at a cost of only $1,000 a mile. Why should we not agree to that, instead of laying down a standard specification for Ontario under which $10,000 a mile would have to be the cost?

The member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) has asked me to explain to the committee the minister's reply to the question that I put. I do not think it would be possible for either the minister or myself to explain to the satisfaction of some members of this House the meaning of what the minister said, because I do not think they want to know. All hon. gentlemen who have spoken to-day have said that 'they are in favour of good

roads; yet very many of them opposed the Bill. Now, the answer made by the minister was as plain as I could wish it to be. I simply wanted to know whether it was the intention of the Government to build a trunk road across the continent, or whether it -was the intention to build branch roads where the provinces were building. He made it very clear to me-I do not know whether it is clear to the member for Bed Deer-that the intention was to build branch roads where the provinces needed them. I know that the province of Ontario is building branch roads-not altogether trunk lines1-which are very satisfactory to the farmers. I was surprised to hear my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) say that specifications should be laid down stating what kind of roads are to be built. I point out to him that one mile of road might require one kind of material and another mile, another kind; in one county, one kind of material might be required and in another county, another; and no doubt one province would want one kind of road and another would want another kind. But if we let every one say where he wants these roads located, if we sat in this House until twelve months from to-day we would be just as far on as we are now, because every one would want the roads at their back doors. The proper way is to have the Provincial Governments locate the roads through the county councils and municipalities; then the road's will be built where they ought to be and where the people want them. I am surprised that the answer of the minister was somewhat vague to the member for Red Deer, for whom I have the greatest respect; to me, it was perfectly satisfactory.

I think it is very important that the decision as to what particular kind of road should be built shall be left largely to the provinces. For instance, in British Columbia it would be almost impossible to set any particular standard, because in the valleys of the range country, which consists largely of open land, a dirt road would be satisfactory, but another kind of road would be necessary in the mountain section, and another through the heavy timber land on Vancouver island and on the coast. It is possible that only a pack trail would be required in a new mining section. British Columbia is a large province which is very little developed, and roads are 'required in all sections of it. We have large areas of rich mining land, timber land and farming land

that are not yet supplied with roads. It may surprise you, Mr. Chairman, when I tell you that one-third of Vancouver island has not yet been explored. We know the value of good roads in British Columbia; they have assisted development to a great extent. Once a road is built through a new section-if it is a mining country, we have trails branching off in different directions from the roads-great development takes place. In the coast sections it would be quite possible to build these roads in the winter season. It is very important, in view of the fact that a number of Government works which had been carried on during the war have been discontinued, that during the next few months we should carry on a certain amount of work to furnish with employment during the coming winter the men who had been engaged in these other works.
If we do not do this, we may have bread lines established in some of the coast sections of British Columbia. I think it is rather wide of the mark to talk of this great country being bankrupt on account of the size of our debt. Having regard to our vast resources and to our comparatively small population, we are practically in a better condition now that the war is over than any other belligerent country. I shall have much pleasure in supporting the Bill.

If the province does not enter into an agreement with the Dominion Government, will it get any part of the $80,000, or will it not? Will a province have to spend $160,000 before it can get ,the $80,000 that is alloted to each province?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Since 1912 this Government, as well as the Government which preceded it, has had to work out agreements of this character year by year with the nine provinces of Canada in connection with the Agricultural Aid Act. During all that time we never had any serious difficulty in reaching a reasonable conclusion which was accepted by both sides. It is perfectly true, as a very eminent British

constitutional writer once said, that if all authorities in any State exercised their powers to the full, you could not carry on Government at all.
People must he reasonable; people are reasonable. We would have no desire to impose our absolute will upon the province, and I trust the province would have no desire to impose their absolute will upon us. If we had some suggestion to make we would sit down and discuss it with them; if they had some suggestion which at the first did not commend itself to our judgment they would sit down and discuss it with us. I have not the slightest apprehension that there will be any serious . difficulty, or indeed, any difficulty, in working out these agreements to the reasonable satisfaction of both governments and to the great advantage of the people of the country.

What I want to know is what the policy of this Government would be in regard to the location of the roads, whether they would regard it as their businfess to say where the roads shall be located, or whether the provincial governments would be allowed to build wherever they liked; and whether they would receive the forty per cent provided the road was built to a certain standard. Will this Government quarrel with the provinces over the location of the road?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not expect to quarrel with the provinces at all. But if, for example, the provinces should undertake to spend this money in the construction of a trunk line across the continent, and we did not think that was for the best advantage of the people of this country, we would be at liberty to take the matter up and discuss it with them, and, I hope, convince them that that would not be the best method of carrying out the proposals contained in this Bill.

Would the minister be gbod enough to lend a sympathetic ear to the suggestion of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Mackie) that some provision should be made in the Bill that neither the provincial governments nor the Dominion Government shall use these large expenditures of public money for political purposes. I would suggest to the minister that inasmuch as we have already sat for a considerable time on this Bill we might now report progress and this evening or tomorrow morning he might take up with the hon. member for Edmonton and other members interested the question of amendl Sir Robert Borden. 1
ing the Bill so that one of the serious objections to it may be removed. There is no doubt about this, that td be consistent, if the Government is abolishing patronage in jts expenditure of public money, it is bound to insist that in the expenditure of any moneys it hands over to any provincial government there shall also be no patronage. If it is a crime for the federal Government to recognize patronage in the expenditure of public money and a great many people hold that view, certainly it would be less corrupt for the federal Government to hand over these moneys to the provincial Government to be used for patronage purposes. speechtext:
I would suggest to my hon. friend the Minister of Railways that in the proper place, which I think is in clause 4, there might be an amendment to this effect. Paragraph (a) now reads as follows:

Will the Government not consider my suggestion that the committee now rise and report progress? This is a very important matter and one that cannot be dealt with without a great deal of difficulty. If we had time to consider if we would be in a better condition to deal with it.

servatives in the province are on the board, appointed by the Prime Minister of Nova Scotia, such men as Colonel Cantley, an out-and-out life-long and leading Conservative of Nova Scotia. There is also a gentleman named Black. I do not know the man, but he is a leading Conservative in the county of Cumberland. There are four men altogether on the board. The Minister of Roads in Nova Scotia, Hon. Mr. Wickwire, whom the Prime Minister knows very well, directs the affairs, but the board is absolutely non-political. There need therefore be no fear of any road expenditure in Nova Scotia being used for political purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member will observe that provision is made in the amendment for cases in which the work cannot conveniently or with avantage to the public interest be carried out by tender and contract, but it is desirable that the reasons should be stated in eacji case, and each Government should consent. If it is a fair case, there is no difficulty about stating the reasons and there need be no apprehension that both Governments will not give their consent.

This will render still more difficult an agreement between the province and the Dominion Government. In-Quebec, in most -cases, the roads are built by the municipalities under agreement with the Provincial Government. Either the municipalities borrow money from the Provincial Government under a special law which has -been passed, the money to be paid back within forty years; or they build the ro.ad and the Provincial Government pays fifty per cent of the cost of construction. The ratepayers work on- the roads under supervision of the officers of the municipal council. How will the new clause work in such a case?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not nearly so familiar as my hon. friend is with the arrangements in Quebec, tout I venture to think that no_ arrangements ought to exist in any province which would prevent large public -works such as are contemplated in this Bill from toeing constructed under: tender and contract. That is the practice in Federal affairs. It is, I think, the practice ordinarily in- provincial affairs, andi there is no reason why the construction of a series of public highways should he made an exception to that rule.	.

Not only the Provincial Government hut the municipalities will he at the mercy of this Government, be-<

cause the roads are ibuilt by 'the municipali-i ties-, which will have to agree to give corn tract by tender. I am not speaking against. this mode of proceeding, I think it is the best mode; hut wha't I object to is the principle 'tlhat is involved in the whole maf^ ter, that the provinces, for a work which is within the provincial jurisdiction, will have to submit to the will, or even the whim, of the Minister of Railways as to, the way in which a provincial work shall be carried out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is not the
whim of the Minister of Railways. The matter is under the disposition of the Governor in Council, because it is the Governor in Council that must finally determine the terms of the agreement. The minister will, of course, in the first place enter into negotiations with proper minister representing the Provincial Government, but in the final1 analysis, so far as the expenditure of this money out of the Federal Treasury is concerned, the responsibility and determination will be with the Governor in Council. I appreciate all that my hon. friend has said about conditions in Quebec, but I should venture to hope that any practice existing there might be so moulded as to conform with the reasonable requirements of this Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have not considered very attentively the details of administration under this Act, but naturally, if there is to be supervision and an inquiry about location, the Federal Government must have the report of some officer in whose judgment it will repose confidence, and that officer must either be resident in British Columbia or be sent there for the purpose.
Will the Prime Minister tell me wherein he thinks is the material difference between; the clause as it appear in the printed Bill and as now suggested in the amendment?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is quite right in one respect if I understand what he has in mind. The Governor in Council, under the section as originally drafted1, can make it a condition of the agreement that the money should be expended by tender and contract. My proposal sets it forth explicitly and defines it; that is all.

I do not anticipate the difficulties of coming . to an agreement which some hon. gentlemen suggest, as between the Provincial and the Federal authorities. On the contrary, I anticipate every desire on both sides to make an agreement. But while I favor the idea of tender and contract generally in public works, I am somewhat doubtful whether you can construct roads in this country to any great extent by tender and contract system. I am a little afraid that the motion that the hon. gentleman has made with the best purposes may complicate matters and make it more difficult. It seems to me that the clause as it stood gave the Government power to put in the agreement, if necessary, "tender and contract" where the conditions would allow. The very purpose of this Bill is to allow some degree of elasticity. If it were possible to have a standard road for the whole Dominion, I presume the minister would have inserted that provision. It is because conditions are not the same in the different Provinces that he has wisely, I think, provided for some measure of elasticity in order that he may adapt himself to the conditions of ea<Jh Province. I am very much afraid that by insisting upon tender and contract here yon may be creating difficulties which will1 not be helpful.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I hardly feel
that the point which my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) makes has the significance, or will involve the danger, which he appears to apprehend. He very correctly points out that it would be within the powers of the Federal Government to make that a stipulation in every agreement. Perhaps I was a little hasty a moment ago when I said that there was no material distinction between the subsection as originally proposed and my amendment. There is this distinction, that in any case where tender and contract is departed from the reasons for such departure must be set out in the Order in Council. My hon. friend will remember that that is a practice which is pursued in regard to public works. In the ordinary course of administration in federal affairs, where tender and contract is departed from the reasons are set out in the Order in Council. When I framed the Order in Council establishing the War Purchasing Commission some four years ago last spring I inserted in that Order in Council a provision which has been in force ever since, that goods and supplies must be purchased by tender and contract except for reasons set forth in the report of the War Purchasing Commission and embodied in
\

the Order in Council. I am bound to say that we found that a very wholesome practice.

In the case of a public work such as a building, a canal or the construction of a section of railway, there is not much difficulty in providing plans and specifications upon which tenders may be called but with the construction of a road, and still more with the repair of a road, it is not by any means such an easy matter. The object is all right-I do not wish to oppose it-but it seems to me that the same purpose could be effected by leaving the Bill as it stood.

While this amendment as proposed by the Prime Minister does not remove by any means all the objections I have to the measure, I think it improves it in a 'substantial degree. It will perhaps free the proposition from some of its most objectionable features. I think it will reasonably ensure that the money will be actually expended in road-making and that such a number of flagrant acts of partisanship as characterized the administration of roads in certain provinces may be eliminated under the Bill as amended. I have strictly refrained in the remarks I made previously from saying anything at all about the administration of road moneys in the province of Nova Scotia.	I thought
that hon. members opposite, being thoroughly	seized	of the	facts and
in consideration of my quiescence on the subject, would have thought it best not to refer to the matter. But the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) has gravely assured this House that there was no need of such a provision in reference to the province of Nova Scotia, and that the moneys of that province were administered in a perfectly non-partisan manner. He stated that the moneys are expended on roads by a road board composed of five members of which Mr. Black, of Cumberland, was a Conservative and consequently that was a guarantee that there was no partisanship in the road moneys of the province of Nova Scotia. Mr. Black, I believe is a Conservative and a member of the road board, but I wish to say that the county of Cumberland, is the only county where any moneys are allowed to be expended through the hands of Conservatives. The county of Cumberland is the only county where the highway inspector is a Conservative or may he presumed to be anything else but a strong advocate of that partisanship to which my hon. friend refers. In the county of Annapolis last year,
out of something like $40,000 ihich was expended, less than $300 was expended through the medium of the Unionist or members of the Union Government, and any supporter of the Unionist party at the last election was not regarded as eligible even to contribute a horse or a cow to the work of constructing roads. In other counties the proportion is worse still. In Pic-tou out of some $60,000 that was spent less than $50 was expended through the medium of supporters of the Union Government. When the hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition made the statement he did he was either saying something which was intended as a joke or something which was contrary to the facts.

Colonel Cantlie, who
was selected by this Government as one of the ablest representative gentlemen in the whole Dominion of Canada to sit on the Munitions Board or to act in connection with the handling of munitions in times of war was a member of this board. I do not think that the hon. member for Annapolis would regard him as a joke upon any' board upon which he was placed in that province. Colonel Cantlie is one of the captains of industry in this country, a man who has made his mark not only in the province of Nova Scotia but in the whole Dominion. I do not know who Mr. Black is, but as I understand it he is a representative Conservative. Mr. Walter Crowe of Sydney, who cannot be classed as a wild Liberal, is a third member of that board, a man who supported the Union party in the last election. I understand, mild politician that I am, that the whole Government of Nova Scotia at the last election unanimously and enthusiastically supported the Union Government and the Union party. They have a very live, active, capable opposition in the Legislature of Noya Scotia. It is a pity for the Conservative party in Nova Scotia that my hon. friend for Annapolis cannot be in both Houses at the same time. He no doubt regards Mr. Hall, leader of the Opposition, and such men as Mr. Hector Mclnnes who represents the city of Halifax, and other men of that calibre, as very bright gentlemen.
I would ask my hon. friend, if within the last ten .years, he has at any time heard any serious complaints from these gentlemen of how Premier Murray has handled the moneys of the province of Nova Scotia spent on the roads. Those are the men who are entrusted by the people of Nova Scotia with authority to look after their affairs. I do admit,

of course,-it is a sad. fact-that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davidson) cannot be everywhere ' and represent the whole business. He has to be here, and as the Irishman said, "A man cannot be in two places at the same time unless he be a bird."
He would have to be a "bird" to do that.

He is a "bird," with nice plumage. I do not wish to labour the point, but only to give sufficient explanation to put the mind of my hon. friend at ease, and to give the assurance that in the province of Nova Scotia we are too busy with lots of other industries, as the hon. gentleman himself knows, to resort to any dealings to get a few days' work on the roads. The problem at the present time in Nova Scotia is to get men to work on the road. The problem does not consist in getting the work to do, but to secure the men to do the work. There was a time, some twenty or thirty years ago, when a few days' work on the roads was a matter of some importance to people who were in need of a little money. But conditions have changed, and to-day the farmer and the miner are too busy in their respective occupations to give their services to this work, and the trouble is to get anybody to do it. I am anxious that this money shall be placed at the disposal of the very excellent committee I spoke of, under the direction of the Minister of Roads and Bridges for the province of Nova Scotia, and under the general supervision of the Murray administration. I might say that the hon. gentleman himself has to-day borne testimony of the highest kind to the Government of Nova Scotia. We had fourteen years of Liberalism in that' province under the direction of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), and since he has stepped out [DOT] of the provincial administration, tiwenty-three years of Liberalism under Premier Murray. And my good friend from Annapolis (Mr. Davidson), says that in these difficult times of financial storm and stress our bonds sold on the market the other day at 103, a premium of $3, instead of selling below par. That sort of testimony comes from a source that is not prejudiced in favour of the government of Nova Scotia. During those two periods of 14 years and 23 years- of Liberal government there has not been one black mark against anybody who had anything to do with the administration of the affairs of that pro-

vince. The provincial administration will therefore not think it worth while to sully that splendid reputation by looking for any little advantage it -might possibly make out of the expenditure of this money.

How far will this agreement apply in the improvement or construction of highways-? The clause we are considering says that a highway shall be constructed or improved in accordance with the terms of an agreement to be entered into. Does that mean that the money can lie spread over a great portion of a highway without building any real permanent thoroughfare?

What that means is this: There may be some existing highway, or old highway at present in use, and the provincial authorities may deem it proper to spend the money on it and bring it up to standard rather than to build a new highway. In that event, the representatives of the two Governments would confer and come to an agreement as to how much should be expended on that particular road in order to make it a good passable highway.

I will give a further illustration, in order to get a true understanding as to what the minister means by the provision. For example, we will say there are in the province of Prince Edward Island 8,000 miles of road. I do not know what the cost of the upkeep of a road is per mile, but we will say that it costs $10, and the money to be voted under this grant amounts to $25 per mile. Would the minister, or the Governor in Council, agree to expend $25 a mile on the old roads for improvement?	.	,

I understand that in Prince Edward Island there is a road commissioner who supervises the expenditures upon roads. The commissioner for the Dominion would consult with the provincial commissioner and the former would submit a proposition to the latter as to where and how the money should be spent. I have no doubt at all the commissioners could come to an agreement. Then we would pay our proportion of forty per cent and the province its proportion of sixty per cent of the total amount to be expended on such road.
Or on the improvement of any road?
Yes.
The question of improvement is covered by the definition in section 2 of the Bill.
Yes.

The leader of the Opposition spoke of the membership of the provincial highway board. It is true that Mr. Black is a Conservative, but where did Colonel Cantlie get.his Conservative principles? Was he not the strongest friend E. M. Macdonald had in the county of Pictou every time he ran? 1 ask my hon. friend if during the time Colonel Cantlie was General Manager for the Nova Scotia Steel Company he can point to one incident of importance as showing him to be a Conservative? If he can, will he please give that information?

I would like to know to
what section the hon. gentleman is speaking.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the point of
order is well taken. It is true that two hon. gentlemen a moment ago engaged in a discussion respecting political affairs in the province of Nova Scotia. member answers the hon. gentleman who is now speaking there would be further discussion on a subject that is entirely irrelevant. The line must be drawn somewhere, and I draw it now. I therefore declare the hon. gentleman out of order.

been submitted tc them, but several of the provincial representatives have been in Ottawa since this Bill was placed on the Order Paper, and as far as I can learn every representative was quite satisfied with the proportion provided for in the Bill. Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 177, to amend the Judges Act.

Before the Bill is read a second time, while I do not want to be understood as objecting to the increase of salaries of the various judges, I do certainly object to this departure from the principle we have always heretofore followed, namely, that the salaries of the judges of one province should not be adjusted unless the question was dealt with for the whole Dominion. I want to state that the line of conduct followed by the Government this year of adjusting the salaries of the judges in the several provinces with the exception of the province of Quebec, should serve as a precedent for future years and that if ever we want to adjust the salaries of the judges of Quebec it will not be taken as an objection that the salaries of the judges in the other provinces are not being reopened. I do this because I have asked the successive Ministers of Justice to remedy the
10 p.m. evil which I have pointed out on previous occasions when this question came before the House, and the ansvper that I invariably got was the one which I have just stated-that if the thing was done for Quebec it would have to be

done for the whole Dominion. But to-day just the reverse happens: it is done for the whole of the Dominion and Quebec is ignored. I just want to register my protest, but I will not go any further for the present.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and the House went into Committee on the Bill. Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 11-Judges not to retire on pensions after 15 years' service or for infirmity unless retirement in public interest, present judges excepted.

The hon. the Acting
Minister of Justice is aware of the point that was raised as to the conditions upon which a judge may retire. I do not think it is reasonable that a judge should be at liberty to retire at his own sweet will. I think a judge or any other public official might reasonably claim superannuation when he has- reached an advanced age, or when he is disabled by physical or mental condition. I cannot imagine any other conditions on which a judge has a right to retire on a pension. The point was raised the other day and I had hoped the hon. minister would deal with it in his Bill.
, CMr. MEIGHEN:	I think the point the
hon. member raises is covered by section 11 of the Bill.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Hitherto the Act in this regard read that the Governor in Council may retire a judge of a Superior Court after fifteen years service on a two-thirds pension. I have not the Act before me, but I know the word. " may " is used. It is very strongly argued, and I believe the argument has been conceded in the past, that though the word " may " is used, the effect is to give an absolute right of retirement on the two-thirds pension after the fifteen years, irrespective entirely of public interest. The amendment therefore in section 11 is to the effect that no such absolute right shall hereafter accrue, but that in determining whether or not retirement may be permitted after fifteen years the Governor in Council may decide on the question of public interest alone. The public interest would be served, I should imagine, should the applicant for retirement be in such ill-health as to prevent the proper discharge of his duties, or should it have been demonstrated, through an act of impeachment or otherwise, that he was unfit for the post he occupies. I am asking the House to continue the provision, hut to

give the right of retirement only on the condition that it is deemed by the Governor in Council to be in the public interest.

The difficulty is in determining what is the interpretation of the phrase "deemed to be in the public interest." I do not want to be personal, but would it be in the public interest that a judge who is in the best of health and strength should retire on pension and immediately proceed to engage in the ordinary affairs of life? That has happened; worse than that has happened, to which I do not wish to allude. If the hon. gentleman can give us the assurance that no judge will be permitted to retire unless he is infirm, physically or mentally disabled, then I shall accept that provision; but it has not been the practice of the past.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It has not been the practice of the past, beoause, I understand, the wording of the clause as it has read in the past gives the absolute right of retirement, the Governor in Council having no discretion in the matter; that is, the judge himself can say whether or not he chooses to retire after fifteen years. This amendment gives discretion to the Governor in Council, based on the public interest. Of course, I could not in any way bind the Governor in Council in respect to the present Administration, much less in respect to a future Administration. But by this Act the duty will be placed upon the Governor in Council to find affirmatively that it is in the public interest that the man retire, before he can choose to retire and succeed in doing so. Wlhat would govern the Governor in Council in that matter is for the Governor in Council, of course, to say, hut if the judge was capable, physically and mentally, of discharging his dutiesi, it could not be in the public interest to retire him, unless there were more judges in the court in question than were necessary.

That is one phase of the question; I ask my hon. friend's attention, then, to the other point, upon which I think there is very strong opinion in the House. Need I again speak about the question of exemptions?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No reasonable objection can be made to repealing the clause as to exemption so far .as it is applicable to. judges whose salaries are raised by this Bill.
Will my hon. friend propose such an amendment to this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Is there any provision in the Exchequer Court Act that one of the judges of that court shall he conversant with both official languages of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I could not answer that question without having the Act before me,
I scarcely think that there is such a provision in the Act, because until very lately there was only one judge of the Exchequer Court; an assistant judge was added five or six years ago. Of course, the assistant judge does understand both , languages.	*

But would it not be wise to provide for the future? There are to be two puisne judges, besides the President of the Court. Why hot insert' an amendment to provide that one of these judges shall be conversant with the two official languages of Canada?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That might be wise, and might not. The purpose of this Bill is not to. deal with the constitution of courts or the character of the men to be appointed, but to deal with the remuneration. If that *end ought to- be achieved, it might be better to do it by amendment to the Exchequer Court Act.
You are amending the Exchequer Court Act to the extent of making provision for an additional judge. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are simply providing salary for an additional judge by an amendment to the Judges Act.
How are you going to appoint a third judge unless you provide that the constitution of the court shall be three judges? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Unless the Exchequer Court Act enables the Governor in Council to appoint a third judge, he cannot be appointed. This merely provides a salary for him when he is competently appointed.
And the Governor in Council does the rest?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is very probable that that is the way it is done.	[DOT]
Why is the senior judge of the Exchequer Court designated as "The President of the Exchequer Court" while other senior judges receive the name of " Chief Justice"?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is the title given to the head of the Exchequer Court in England; it is believed by a judge of the Exchequer Court to be the appropriate title.
Section 11 agreed to.
On motion of Mr. McKenzie the committee reverted to section 10-salaries increased $1,000 each.	*

I directed the attention of the minister last night to the fact that he was adding $1,000 to the salaries of County Court judges. The County Court judges of the districts of Halifax and St. John receive $3,500, and, as the flat rate seems to be established by this Bill at $4,000, these judges would not, under the Bill as it stands, get an increase of $1,000. If that was an oversight, I trust the minister will put it right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There was no oversight at all. It is true that in certain cities the senior County Court judge has been receiving a salary of $3,500; in such cases the addition to the salary under this legislation will be only $500. I do not know that I can give with certainty the names of the cities in which these judges receive $3,500, but they include, I think, St. John, Halifax, Toronto, Ottawa, Hamilton, and perhaps one or two others.
But the city of Winnipeg was not such a place, Regina was not such a place, Calgary was not, and so forth. Usually the capital of the province was the city where the extra $500 was given; but that was not always so. Nor, indeed, were it so, could it be held to warrant its discontinuance, for the reason that there were other cities, in some cases as large, or even larger, than the capital of the province in which it would be- inequitable to deny the senior judge the additional salary he would receive in the capital of the province. Consequently, I thought it would be better to make a round salary of $4,000 applicable everywhere, and then to endeavour to meet inequalities that might exist by a rearrangement of jurisdictions such as is now being provided for in Ontario, and such as I think should be provided for in every province. Hereafter every county or district court judge will obtain exactly the same salary from the treasury of Canada, $4,000. That means an increase of $1,000 almost universally, but in some cases it means just $500 increase. I believe the average county court judge's salary in Ontario from the Dominion was $3,006. That will illustrate how very few there were who were getting over $3,000. To give effect to the suggestion of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's

(Mr. Fielding), I beg to move that section 13 be added to the. Bill to read as follows:
13. The provisions of subsection 3 of section 27 shall not apply to any judge' whose salary is increased by this Act.

Is the definition of "income " in the Income Tax Act broad enough to include a judge's salary?
Mr, MEIGHEN: As I recall it, the Income Tax Act provides that it shall apply to the salaries of all judges appointed after the passing of that Act. The effect of the amendment will be to make the Income Tax Act or any other tax or deduction imposed under any Act of the Parliament of Canada applicable to all judges whose salaries are increased by this statute.
How does subsection 3 of section 27 read?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As follows:
The salaries and retiring allowances or annuities shall be payable by monthly instalments and shall be free and clear of all taxes and deductions whatsoever imposed under any Act of the Parliament of Canada.
The amendment I moved provides that that section shall not apply to any judge whose salary is increased by this Act.
By this amendment will not my hon. friend be depriving these judges of their monthly instalments? .

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is correct. My amendment should have read:
The provisions of subsection 3 of section 27 as to taxes and deductions shall not apply to any judge whose salary is increased by this Act.

Is not the minister
going further than was suggested either by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) or my hon. friend ifrom Precott (Mr. Proulx)? I understand that their contention was that only the amount to be added to the judges' salaries should be subject to taxation, but that we should stand by the bargain we made with the judges. The minister is abandoning that idea altogether and making the whole salary taxable. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) will remember that his contention was as I have said.

I am bound to say that the minister has given effect to my views.
I can see no reason why we should tax one part of the salary and not the other. What we are doing is this: We are recognizing what somebody has called a contractual arrangement; we are recognizing a vested right on the part of certain judges; we do not disturb that right, but we say that as

respects judges whose salaries will be affected by this Act we will remove the exemption. The Income Tax Act also declares that there shall be no exemption as regards judges appointed in the future. The net result will be that a few judges who are not affected by this legislation will enjoy the exemption, and until something happens by which we are doing something for them I am content they should have the exemption.

The discussion we have had goes for nothing if we are going to take away the exemption. What we said the other day was that we should stand by the statute which exempted the salary of a judge from any imposts of any kind. Everybody will agree to that, particularly the hon. member for Kingston, who said that a contract was a contract and we had to stand by it. Now we are breaking that contract, arid we are making the whole salary subject to taxation because we are giving the judges a slight increase. We must know exactly what we are doing. We are absolutely repealing the exemption which judges are supposed to have. If it is distinctly understood that we are going back on our contract, I have nothing more to say, except that we did hold out in a most virtuous manner the other day that we should stand by that contract, and that there would be no "scraps of paper" in this country so far as we are concerned. But now we are absolutely scrapping that statute so far as its exemption provisions are concerned, and we are making the judges whom we have exempted for the last fifty years liable to taxation; We are breaking the contract we made with them. If that is the will of this Committee all right, but we must understand exactly what we are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I understood the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens just as he states his own understanding is to-day, nor do I consider the reasoning of the leader of the Opposition good, that this involves any breach of contract - whatsoever; it has not even the colour of it. The statute contained a provision that when any judge was appointed he should receive a salary of $3,000, let us say, and that that salary should be exempt from taxation. So long as we do nothing which takes away from that man's salary of $3,000, surely we cannot be said to have broken any contract with him. The total effect of our action is to add to his salary. So far from breaking the contract we have added to the contract in his favour; that is all we

, are doing. Certainly the taxation that would be imposed on the whole salary would be a .mere fraction of the increase we are giving now.

Yes, hut a salary is a salary whether it is $3,000 or $10,000, and we -made a contract with the judges that their salaries would be exempt from imposts of any kind. Now we propose to give them an increased salary, not free from taxation. We are therefore changing the condition.
If we take away an exemption worth $200 or $300 and give him $1,000 instead, I cannot see where we are doing any harm.

It has been well said in the discussion on the Bill that it might have been all right to have such a commission during the war; but we are not now legislating for war conditions; but for peace. The Bill provides for the absorption of the existing staffs in this new branch of the public service, which would mean the consolidation of the purchasing staffs in the various departments in one central purchasing department. I quite agree with my hon. friend that an employee who has been rendering faithful and efficient service to the country for many years should not be turned adrift because of some Change in the form of administration. In so far as they are not required in this centralized purchasing board, they would be drafted info other positions in other branches of the service. It is not contemplated, and it is not expected, that there will be any increase in the number of employees in connection with the work of this department. On the contrary, as soon as the department is organized and working efficiently it follows as a natural consequence

that you can do the work in one office with one set of officials with a smaller number than when the work is done with many sets of officials. Common ordinary business sense will show us that is the case, and that is the policy pursued by business men in the large business concerns of Canada.
Another very important consideration-one of the most important, in fact,-is that Government supplies can be purchased to better advantage if they are bought in large quantities and under the conditions mentioned in the Bill, than if they are purchased in small quantities to meet the needs from time to time of a particular department. The Bill contemplates all departments anticipating their needs and presenting their recommendations to the purchasing Commission; and where there are several departments requiring the same class of supplies the Commission will be able to effect a large saving, jusit as any for all branches of the Government at the best possible terms at which they can secure those supplies, and thereby should be able to effect a large saving, just as any merchant when purchasing in large quantities is able to do so at a lower rate than the man who has to buy only in small quantities.
Now let me mention another important
aspect of this question that I did not refer to before, and when the Bill goes back into Committee I intend to move an amendment to give effect to it: One of the important recommendations of the Joint Industrial Committee in Great Britain was, in the case of the British Government, that the Government should purchase its supplies through one central purchasing department under such conditions as would tend to provide against unemployment. In other words, it should so place its orders as to ensure, so far as the Government could in any way ensure, employment under conditions where otherwise there might be unemployment, that is, place its orders at such a period of the year, and under such conditions, as would help to mitigate the dangers of unemployment. Let me read to my hon. friend from the report of the Industrial Relations Commission in Great Britain, a paragraph in reference to this matter:	.
3. Stabilizing Employment.-In order to provide against the fluctuating demand' for labour, the Committee think that the Government should undertake the definite duty of stimulating the demands for labour in bad times by postponing contracts of a non-urgent character until it is necessary to promote a demand for labour owing to falling trade. For this purpose, in allocating Government orders, consideration should, of course, be given to the circumstances
of the industry concerned. The Committee are of opinion that much more effective action could be taken if all orders for particular classes of commodities were dealt with by one Government department. It would further be an advantage in order that the policy which they have indicated should be carried out, that all Government contracting should be supervised by one authority. Local authorities should be urged to adopt a similar policy with regard to work under their control.
This covens more than the purchase of supplies, it covers the totting of Government contracts. It embodies this important principle that the Government, as one of the chief business organizations of the [DOT]country, should so place its orders for material and supplies as to guard, so far as any large institution can do so, against unemployment by providing employment, at the period when it is most needed.

That in purchasing supplies for the puDlio service the commission shall have regard, so far as reasonably practicable, to the general state and prospects of the labour market, with the object of reducing unemployment due essentially to periodical fluctuations in industry.

I will read a paragraph from the Prime Minister's address to the country on November 10, 1917, which followed the announcement of the general election and the appeal to'the country:
But there are other reasons why the Union Government should be entrusted with power. It has pledged itself to the extirpation of old abuses, and to a wise and bold policy of constructive reform. The system of patronage in the distribution of contracts and offices which has prevailed in Canada for generations has been the root of many political evils. It has fostered local and sectional interest incompatible with the national welfare and injurious to the efficiency of the national services. It has troubled representatives of the people, permitted the ascendancy of organized minorities in the constituencies, and affected the independence of Parliament itself. It may be that these evils should have been overcame long ago. Censure may lie upon successive governments which have tolerated the system, but inveterate diseases succumb only to heroic treatment-and heroism has not distinguished Canadian parties in dealings with patronage. Generally, govern-

ments have lived long in Canada, and when for many years distribution of patronage has been confined to the party in power there is a natural disposition to adjust the balance when at length the other party succeeds to office. Once committed to the system, influences are recognized and interests created that are not easily resisted or dislodged. It is believed that a government derived from both political parties and strengthened by special representation of agriculture and organized labour, can act with greater freedom and independence than a government which held office under the old conditions. Hence the resolution to abolish trading in patronage, to fill public offices by merit and not by favouritism, and to establish honest and open competition in awarding contracts and buying supplies.

speechtext: I am surprised that my hon. friend has brought this measure forward this evening. subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: I beg my hon. friend's pardon; if he so interpreted my remarks, he misunderstood me. I said that this was carrying out an election pledge. subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: There is not much difference between the interpretation that I placed upon my hon. friend's words and what he has just said. He contends this evening, as he did the other evening, that this commission is the outcome of an election pledge given in 1917 by the Prime Minister when he and his party went to the country. Let us not deceive ourselves with words, if you please. It has been stated here to-day, and no one can gainsay the assertion, that at the last general election the one cry, the one slogan, was " Win the war.' The (Government carried the election on that cry, on that slogan, and on no other. No one in the many audiences which were addressed by my hon. friend during the course of that campaign

subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: Even in the churches

subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
No one in the churches or in the public halls, will recall that the Government sought to impress the electors with the necessity of creating this commission. To the people of the country this proposal is a novelty. True, the people understand perfectly well that during the war, commissions might reasonably be created in order to assist in carrying on the war successfully. As I stated the other evening, I have nothing whatever to say against the gentlemen who were the members of the



War Purchasing Commission. I happen to know one of them, Sir Hormisdas Laporte, for whom I have the highest regard. In carrying out the work assigned to him during the war period, Sir Hormisdas Laporte has rendered valuable service to the country. But the war is now over; we are living under conditions of peace, and the country is faced with a huge national debt. If my hon. friend wishes to live up to the expectations of his friends, he must accustom himself to rigid, economy during the next few years; he must even do some cheeseparing, because the country is not in a mood to maintain in office any Government that will play with the national finances.
The creation of this new commission will entail the organization of a large personnel and will involve the country in a very large expenditure. Remember that when I say "large expenditure," I do not mean millions; we must stop counting millions as lightly as we have counted them during the war period. In the normal times of a few years ago, a few hundred thousand dollars meant a great deal to this country, and I submit that under present circumstances a few hundred thousand dollars will count for a great deal in the administration of our national finances. The Government must face stern realities. The Minister of Fin-ancte cannot now expect to obtain millions out of domestic loans with the same facility that he obtained them during the war, because now that peace has come, the people expect the Government to call a halt on large expenditures.
I do not oppose this measure because of any desire that patronage should not be abolished. It is my sincere hope and wish that patronage be abolished. I freely grant that it has been the curse of the land. But let the ministers first reform themselves. Alphonse Karr, the famous writer, speaking on one occasion against the abolition of the death penalty, coined a phrase which since has often been repeated: "Que messieurs les assassins commencent eux- memes"-let the murderers themselves begin first to secure the abolition of the death penalty. If the Government is so anxious to abolish patronage, let the ministers of the Crown begin by reforming themselves. They did not take their oath of office to maintain or to facilitate patronage; when they were sworn as ministers of the Crown, they promised faithfully under the eye of God, that they would be fair, that they would be honest, that they would have more regard for the finances of the

country than for their own personal finances.
A minister of the Crown is not selected by the Prime Minister, does not enjoy the confidence of the majority in the House, because, forsooth, he can deliver academic orations. The people expect a minister of the Crown to be an administrator, to be given the direction of a department, and it is his duty to look after the business of that department. He must not run about the country from one end to the other, except on occasions when his presence is needed in order to carry on affairs of State. If he knows how to practice economy, when he travels in this democratic country he should travel like the rest of us mortals travel. There is nothing, for instance, in his oath of office which compels a minister of the Crown to use private cars, and to delay or block ordinary passenger traffic. A minister of the Crown must administer his department faithfully and as economically as possible in the best interests of the people; The very name of "minister" signifies administration. It comes from the Latin "ministrare" to administer, not from "orare," to pray, or deliver academic orations. My hon. friend has not a spending department, but let us take his colleagues, the Minister of Railways and Canals, the Minister of Militia and Defence, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the Minister of Public Works-they are at their office every day looking after the administration of their respective departments and receiving the requests that are made by the people. They must consult with the officials of the department and with the deputy minister, and when any expenditure has to be made, the requisition, O.K.'d by the deputy comes before the minister. If he is anything like a minister he does not require the services of three highly-paid commissioners in a different building surrounded by a host of officers, also highly paid, in order to pass judgment on the purchase of desks, paper, and the several articles that are needed in his department.

subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: How does the hon. gentleman apply that in connection with the Civil Service Commission, and in the appointment of officials?

subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
The report which the Civil Service Commission have had prepared by an American firm is such a muddle -I don't say model-that it has been discarded by the Government and will not be submitted to the House this session. It

will probably be buried and we shall never hear of it again. That commission was to reorganize and improve everything in connection with the Civil Service, and what has it accomplished? Let us consider first things first. I say that an honest minister has in the Act governing his department all the machinery necessary to conduct honestly and efficiently the affairs of his department. And here is exactly the point I wish to impress upon the House. We are living in this country under British methods of government, but I say that we are departing very widely from those time-honoured administrative methods. During the war they had several commissions in England. They had to appoint commissions, as we had to, in order to carry on the business of the country, because the war created a pressure of business that no ten or twenty ministers of the Crown could possibly undertake. But do you believe that Mr. Lloyd-George will maintain during the peace period which is now opening any of the commissions which were specially created during the war? I daresay that not one of them will be maintained now that peace has been signed. The British people would not stand for any such departure from the principle of government.
My hon. friend stated a moment ago that the commission which presented the famous Witley Report recommended to the British Government that the purchasing of all supplies be concentrated in the hands of one body, so as to allay as much as possible the unrest caused by unemployment. My hon. friend made there exactly the point which in my judgment should condemn the very legislation before us to-night. The system of government in England is quite different from ours; I do not say that the administrative methods are different, but that the system is. England has only one central government for the British Isles. It is, relatively speaking, only a narrow fringe of territory, and the British Government looks not only after Imperial works, not only after national works, but even local and municipal works. That is one of the reasons why to-day in conservative England, much to my pleasure, they are advocating the decentralization of power. You may read in the press-I read of the scheme many years ago in some historic letters published in the London Times and emanating, if I mistake not, from one of the leading constitutional authorities in England-that possibly within the next few months a radical plan of decentralization will be presented to the Parliament of the
282i
United Kingdom. There will be one local government for Wales, another for Scotland, another for Ireland-be not afraid, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to introduce the Home Rule question in this debate. The tendency in England to-day is to decentralize government. I can quite understand that in the Old Country, considering the variety and magnitude of the work to be accomplished, it is necessary to centralize the purchasing activities of the Government under one authority. My hon. friend forgets that there is a standing army in England and a navy unequalled in the world. It means several hundred millions of expenditure, and I can understand that under these circumstances the British Government should think of centralizing the purchasing power of the Government. It is a small country, territorially speaking, with a large population and with one central Government, a system which is obsolete. But here, in Canada, the conditions are quite different. It is true we have the Dominion Government at Ottawa, but we have a large territory. We have to deal with half a continent, comprising nine provinces. Will my hon. friend undertake to convince me that when the Chief Engineer of the Public Works Department in British 'Columbia requires some instruments for his officers, or possibly some steel or timber for some of the government works, he will have to apply to Ottawa in order to receive his directions from that extraneous body? If he had to consult any one, it would be first the Minister of Public Works or the Chief Engineer of the Public Works Department, or the Deputy Minister. No. Conditions are not parallel as between Canada and Great Britain,	and	the argument	of my hon,friend in	that	regard falls to	the ground.'My hon. friend in referring to the report on the industial conditions of the country, said that he would insert a section in the Bill to meet the suggestion concerning purchases which. is found in the Witley Report. But he has not said that the Government had accepted the report of the majority. There are two reports. There is the report of	the	majority and	there is thereport of	the	minority. Which of the two
will the Government accept? I know which of the two I would accept, but I must say that the report of the majority covers a very large order and before taking a portion of it and inserting it in the Bill, my hon. friend should first of all-state the policy of the Government as regards the whole of the report. .

I oppose this measure because, first, the country cannot stand any useless expenditures, and, second, the pledge referred to by my hon. friend is no argument at all. The pledge given by the Government during the last campaign was to carry on and to win the war, and the people never understood that once the war was won the Government would continue in operation the various commissions which had been created especially during the course of .the war for a specific purpose. Many people whom I have met of late, belonging to both sides of politics, and many who practically have no politics but are simply business anen, have opened their hearts to me on many occasions since the beginning of the session. Let me say in all sincerity to the right honourable gentleman (Sir Robert Borden) that there are many thousands of people who sympathize with him in his thankless task. Many people sympathize with him and with the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) and I may say frankly, speaking on behalf of those who sit on your left, Mr. Chairman, that not many envy the lot of the right honourable gentleman, or are anxious to take the seals of office during the	present
period of unrest, because we know the	heavy burden which	weighs
on the shoulders of the Prime Minister. We know that from day to day he must ask himself:	How shall we carry on?
What will be the outcome of this great crisis? Is not the credit of Canada very seriously impaired? Our national debt has reached the enormous figure of two billion dollars. We have to provide for the payment of the interest charges. Are not the business men who support the Government .afraid of the heavy responsibility with which the country is being saddled at the present moment? It seems to me that the right honourable gentleman should be firm, staunch and stern, and should turn away from him all those who are importuning him for the creation of new sinkholes of expenditure. Is not the Government going a little too far when, besides an enormous national debt, it has taken over the Canadian Northern and is about to take over the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway .Company? Does this not involve many more millions? And why should the Government strain another point and put on the shoulders of the tax payers such a useless expenditure as is entailed by the creation of this new commission? It is unfortunate that a man like Sir Hormisdas Laporte is not in the Government. If he were, I would say: " Appoint 
him Minister of Purchases, because he is an able business man and an honest man, but let him be responsible to the people." What I do not like about the Bill is that you are creating an irresponsible body. One of the chief functions of Parliament is to control expenditures. Suppose this commission is in existence and a minister of the Crown is charged by members of this House with scandalous expenditures or with corruption. Under this new system the Prime Minister will simply shrug his shoulders and say "We are not responsible; you have created a commission which controls all expenditures, therefore we are not guilty." Is that the British method of Government? Surely not, Mr. Chairman. And for that reason, with many others, I say that the President of the Privy Council should not press this legislation.
There are many Unionists and, I am told, many Cabinet ministers who are bitterly opposed to this legislation. They have no love for this legislation because they fear it will be too costly. I hope that my right hon. friend will, after the discussion that we have had on this measure, postpone it, sleep over it until next session, and consider if there is no other legislation more useful, more pressing, and more in the interest of the country.
Major-General MEWBURN: I have listened to the eloquent speech of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) which, I think, would sound very well in an election campaign. But, let me say that the public of this country are anxious that this Government, or another Government, should get away from the antiquated political method of purchasing supplies. As Minister of Militia my experience has been that the War Purchasing Commission, as constituted, has been the means of effecting the very greatest savings to this country. In that department it is true we have most efficient contract branch and inspection branches, but all war supplies, equipment, clothing and other things that have been needed for the soldiers have been purchased .through the War Purchasing Commission, and I am satisfied from the experience I have had that their efforts have resulted in an enormous saving to the country. Since the armistice was signed we have been taking stock in the ordnance department with a view to salvaging, or realizing upon, the surplus supplies on hand. I think I am not overstating it when I say that the War Purchasing Commission have done wonders in this way. I believe that the creation of this

proposed purchasing commission will be in the interest of economy because it means that we are getting down to a proper business basis in the purchase of supplies for the different departments and that they will be properly controlled. Any gentleman who has had any business experience must admit the soundness of that view.
I do not think there is any more efficient organization in the country than the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and one of its most efficient departments is the purchasing department. It is the same with the big department stores and the steel companies; the purchase of supplies is all controlled through their purchasing departments. I quite agree that the minister must not shirk his responsibility to Parliament.
