speechtext:
Who is responsible to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific- the board of directors or the purchasing office i
Major-General MEWBURN: The president is responsible to his directors, but the time of the president is too valuable to waste in checking over supplies. He has trusted employees who purchase these supplies and I venture to say if it were left to the president the purchasing would not be as well or as economically done. That is the record of all large business enterprises and corporations. I am satisfied that if this commission could do the purchasing for all the departments a great many of these branches that we now have under different departments of the Government could be eliminated and the work could be taken care of in the way that is here proposed. I cannot see why we should have in every department a contract and inspection branch. Instead of having fifteen or twenty of such branches you might have one efficient purchasing commission and the faithful employees who are now in these departments could be absorbed into other departments, while those men who are not useful to the country would be better out of the Government service.

subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
I do not wish at this late hour to detain the committee unduly, but there are a few aspects of this question that I would like to treat for a few moments. We are met by this Bill with a proposal to make a very specific change in 'the manner in which purchases are made for the Government. Up to this time I understand a great number of the departments have had their separate purchasing departments.
or purchasing agents. The suggestion is that these should be centralized into one department. I freely grant that that might be an advantage. I am willing to accept the .statement made by the Government that in their opinion it would be an advantage. That is a proposition to which I have no objection ito offer. With the method by which the Government proposes to carry out this proposition I have no serious quarrel. I am not opposed to the idea of a commission; but I say that if it is necessary -and I am inclined to believe it would be advantageous to have a purchasing department-that department should be under the control of a minister having a seat in. this House and that the man who did the actual purchasing should be a civil servant, trusted, honoured, well paid, who would be under a minister in the same way as any other civil servant would be. The minister in introducing this Bill stated that the object of it is to remove from the public Life of this country the curse of patronage I am absolutely in accord with him as to the desirability of .such a change in the condition of affairs being brought about.
The minister has said that he proposes to do this in pursuance of a pledge made at the time of the formation of the Union Government that patronage would be abolished, and he goes on ito read from a manifesto issued by the Prime Minister at that time stating that neither of the political parties had up to that time displayed much heroism in dealing. with patronage, and that was the time for heroism to be displayed. But Mr. Chairman, heroism is not displayed by the pursuit of a fugitive, cloistered virtue. If the ministers wish to show heroism let them organize the department that is proposed and let that department be run without patronage. Do not multiply commissions and do not endeavour to remove the responsibility for purchases from the Government. Do not appoint a practically independent commission. I think the minister who is in charge of this Bill (Mr. Rowell) has been rather affected by the arguments along this line because he suggested his willingness to make a modification. As far as I am concerned, if he will eliminate the idea of a commission, and merely ask for power to create a purchasing department which will be conducted as other department are under our Canadian constitution and in line of British traditions and policy, I will agree to the proposal. But I say that this measure is objectionable. Do not endeavour to cure one evil by starting another. I believe the
COMMONS*
members of this House will be with me when I say that one of the greatest dangers of democracy is the creation of a bureaucracy. This will be just a little bureaucracy. I should not say "a little bureaucracy" because it would be the beginning of a very important bureaucracy. The minister who introduced this Bill or resolution was not exactly annoyed but somewhat affected by the imputations cast from this side of the House upon his desire to eliminate patronage.
The minister said that we on this side would expect no good to come out of Nazareth. I would not like to say that hon. gentlemen on this side regard him as a Messiah sent for the salvation of the Canadian people; we will leave that to admirers of the President of the Privy Council who sit close to him. But let me say this : The minister may feel a little hurt at our attitude; he may regard the Union Government as a fine flower of disinterested patriotism. He shakes his head in mild and humble deprecation. He is right. He should deprecate any such idea, because that is not the view that the Canadian people have of Union Government. They regard Union Government-not all those, of course, who supported it, but the institution itself-as having its origin in the greatest electoral fraud that was ever consummated on the Canadian people, the War-time Elections Act. They regard it as an institution which has been nourished in hyprocrisy, under the pretence that patronage was eliminated when it was not eliminated, and they regard it as having been consummated by a great breach of faith towards the two historic parties of this country. Because I may remind the minister, and others interested in Union Government, that when that Government was formed it was solemnly stated that it was a mere temporary joining of forces for the prosecution of the war in the manner which those persons thought best, but which other people thought not best. And when those who obtained a mandate under such conditions took advantage of the position in which they found themselves to form a party distinct from either of the existing political parties, I assert humbly, and I trust without discourtesy, it was a decided breach of faith with those two great historic parties. If, therefore, we take advantage of the condition as we find it, and if the situation as it presents itself to us to voice our views, the minister must not be surprised when we take his protestations of superior political virtue with a certain accompaniment of salt.

Now, let the minister amend his Bill. I do not believe that he is altogether deaf or altogether unaffected by principles which I am sure were inculcated in him in his youth. I think he can see it is a desirable thing that in a great department of government any person or persons carrying on the public business of the country should be represented by an individual sitting in this House to whom the responsibility for the action of that person or persons may be brought immediately home. I believe the minister in his heart of hearts is with me in that contention, and I would just say this:	-Let him follow
that principle; let him eliminate the idea of a highly-paid bureaucratic independent commission, and let him substitute for it a pur eh; sing department run by a responsible minister with properly paid officials trusted by that minister and whose reputation will make them acceptable to the people, and a great deal of the opposition which he finds to this Bill will disappear.

subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
When
the resolution upon which this Bill is founded was originally submitted for consideration, I was opposed to the appointment of this commission. That resolution was introduced by the President of the Privy Council, and I was reluctant to criticise the provisions embodied therein. I have listened to all the arguments that have been advanced in support of the appointment of the commission, and I am still of the opinion that this is unwise legislation. Our position on this side in respect to this matter is somewhat embarrassed by the President of the Privy Council reading to us to-night from the Union platform in the elections of 1917, and in the statement which he made, when the matter was last before the House, in order to demonstrate that the legislation has been introduced in pursuance of a promise made at that time, and that it establishes a principle which was approved of by the electors in the elections of that year. My own view is in accord with that of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) and the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), that in the elections of 1917 the Canadian people were not bothering themselves very much about a purchasing commission. I myself was not a candidate in that election. Nevertheless, I was more or less active in the support of the candidate for Union Government in the constituency which I now have the honour to represent. During that campaign I took part in many meetings addressed by members of the Government and

members of this House; and I must confess that when it was stated here by the President of the Privy Council that the appointment of this commission was an issue in the elections of 1917, it was my first intimation that such was the fact.
While I oppose the legislation which this Bill seeks to enact, and the resolution upon which it was founded, I desire to dissociate myself from much that has been said by those who like myself are opposed to the measure. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) suggested that if the Bill were adopted the commission for whose appointment it provides would be used for political purposes. _ My own view, of couse, is the exact opposite from that. I also desire to go on record as expressing the opinion that the work done by the War Purchasing Board during the period of the war was very valuable work and in the best interests of Canada. Furthermore, I feel that the criticism of that board which has been indulged in is entirely unwarranted, and that the board's work will be commended by all those who have had any occasion to look into what it has done. But while that is so, we must consider that the work performed by the board was done under abnormal conditions. It would be unreasonable to suppose that the purchasing machinery of this Government prior to the war which started in 1914 would have been adequate and sufficient for the purpose of carrying on the purchasing needed under war conditions. But it does seem to me entirely unnecessary that we should attempt to carry into peace time Government machinery necessitated by the abnormal conditions which have existed during the last four and a half years. With reference to what has been stated, not only to-night, but from time to time as this matter has been under discussion in the House as to the general rules of business, I submit, Mr. Chairman, that in business there is no general rule governing a matter of this kind. I do urge, though, that to-day efficient methods in all lines of commercial and industrial business lead to decentralization and to departmentalization.
Whether it be a. Government or whether it be a manufacturing or industrial institution, the tendency to-day is towards departmental responsibility, and if we take most of the large institutions we shall find that to be the case. The hon. Minister of Militia referred to the Canadian Pacific railway, and undoubtedly the Canadian Pacific railway is the outstanding example in Canada to-day of centralized buying.
But those who are in a position to know will bear me out when I say that the purchasing department of the Canadian Pacific railway reflects the genius of one man, and in all human probability will pass out when he passes. There are other institutions, such as the Massey-Harris, where they have centralized buying; but I would urge that the tendency is towards departmentalization and away from centralization. Reference has been made by the Minister of Militia to the department stores.
I submit that what he states to be the fact there with reference to purchasing is the exact opposite to the practice that actually obtains. There is not a department store to-day in which the purchasing is not done by the head of the department who is responsible for the selling, and I am sure that those who are familiar with business management will realize the necessity of just such a plan. Otherwise it is passible for the man who is responsible for the selling end to pass responsibility over to the purchasing department and say, "I cannot sell your goods because they were poorly bought." It is undoubtedly a fact that in all the department stores in Canada, as well as in the United States, there are as many purchasing heads as there are departments. I can tell the hon. minister that a textile manufacturer will go to-day with a line of samples to the largest department stores in Canada and will sell the same goods to six different men in the institution; and that is the condition in reference to boots and shoes and in reference to almost every line of commodity in which a department store deals. The tendency is exactly in the same direction in manufacturing industries. I admit there is no general rule. There are possibly just as well managed institutions which have centralized buying as there are institutions which have not; but what I do submit is that the tendency of efficient purchasing to-day leads towards departmentalization and away from centralized buying.
This Bill provides for a very elaborate purchasing department-a department which will apparently equal many of the present departments of the Government. It provides for three cpmmissioners, for a director of purchasing, for experts, and for clerks. It is apparently the intention that there shall be continued in peace times as elaborate an organization for the purchasing of what this Government requires as existed during the war. I am not going into the question of ministerial responsibility and the parliamentary view of it. I would hesi-

tate to do so in the presence of so many members who have devoted their lives to parliamentary procedure; in fact, I would regard it as presumptuous on my part to deal with this question from the standpoint of parliament responsiblity. But it is impossible to ignore the fact that the principle involved in this Bill creates a tendency to get away from ministerial responsibility to Parliament. At the present time, as a result of the legislation which was passed last session, if any matter arises on the passing of Estimates dealing with the staffs in any of the departments, the minister holds up his hands and says, and quite rightly: " I have nothing to do with the appointment of the staff in my department, as we have now canonized the deputy ministers, and they alone have to do with the recommendation for dismissal." So we have taken the service entirely out of politics, which may or may not meet with the views , of many hon. members. If the purchasing is now taken out of the hands of the heads of the departments, and if the ministers in this House are no longer responsible for what their departments purchase, then we are again getting away from ministerial responsibility. As has already been said, I think by the hon. mem-
12 m. ber for Maisonneuve, all the amounts that will be required to run the national railways are beyond the control of this House, as they have been passed over to a board. So I submit it would be well that something should be kept within the control of this House. When the matter was last before the House, a very strong argument was advanced in support of this commission by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Harold). He went very fully into the details of what had been done by the War Purchasing Commission, having apparently investigated the activities of the commission for the purpose of supporting this Bill. He told us that he had had an opportunity of looking up the files of the commission, covering, I think an aggregate expenditure of some $200,000,000, and he gave to the House details of certain savings that were effected as a result of the work of that commission, savings ranging in the seven instances he gave from $328.86 to $3,142.80. But I would urge, Mr. Chairman, that it is unfair to take the highest tender and the lowest, and then give to the War Purchasing Commission the credit of having saved the country the difference.

speechtext: I am afraid the hon. gentleman made a mistake. I was only showing the necessity of calling for tenders.

speechtext: I did not so understand the hon. gentleman. But I can see very little difference between what he now states and my statement, for the simple reason that it brings you back to the point that the House is asked to assume that it is necessary to have a commission in order to insure that the lowest tender will be accepted which, I submit, is a promise that we ought not to be asked to accept. It has been urged that i't is necessary to appoint a commission in order to get away from the patronage evil, which it is claimed has heretofore existed in the purchasing for the different departments. I feel that that is a reflection on many honest and capable men employed in the different departments, and if it should be felt that there is some necessity for certain co-ordination in purchasing supplies for the different departments, then I submit, Mr. Chairman, it should surely be possible to work out such co-ordination without establishing practically a new department of Government. This Bill as it stands has certain defects. We were told by the President of the Privy Council when' the matter was last before the House that it was the intention to retain in each department certain purchasing experts to do the requisitioning and that it would be necessary to retain also a number of the members of the purchasing staff in each department for the purposes of inspection after the goods were received.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: My hon. friend must have misunderstood me; I did not so put it. I said that it would be necessary to retain a portion of the staff to make requisitions, but, as I recall the statement I made, I did not say that any portion of the staff, or any experts, should be retained for purposes of inspection.

subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
As it appears in Hansard, a certain number of the staff were to be retained for the purposes of requisitioning and inspection. I took what I said from Hansard; if it is wrong, I withdraw it. But if a certain number of the purchasing staffs of the departments are retained for the purposes of requisitioning, the position will be this: Those who are so retained will be purchasing from the commission and the commission will be purchasing from those who supply. It has been stated that the policy of this Purchasing Commission will be such that when a requisition is sent from a department to

the commission, the precise article that is requisitioned must be purchased. That was explained by the case of the waste paper basket to which reference has already been made. That is, if a two-dollar basket were requisitioned, a two-dollar basket would be purchased; if a forty dollar basket were requisitioned, a forty dollar basket would be purchased. If a wooden desk were requisitioned, a wooden desk would be purchased, and if an iron desk were requisitioned, an iron desk would be purchased. I wish to point out that the whole policy of the manufacturing trade to-day is toward specialization. It is impossible to find any manufactured article, anything that is put up-even if it could formerly have been considered as a staple article- in connection with which the manufacturer does not specialize in some way in order to give to the article or to the product a "talking" or advertising value. The result is that in respect of practically every article that the Government will require, the product of one manufacturer will have certain special features and that same article, turned out by another manufacturer, will have other special features of a different nature. The whole policy of the manufacturers is to adopt something that will make their article just a little different from what anybody else has to sell. If, then, the requisition must be literally followed, the real purchasing in the majority of cases will be done by the man who issues the requisition, and that man will have no responsibility in the matter at all, because he passes on the requisition to the Purchasing Commission, and that requisition can, perhaps, be filled only by one manufacturer or by one commercial house. It seems to me that in this regard our last condition will be worse than our first.
It is urged that in the appointment of this commission we shall be getting away from patronage. I submit that as the requisitioning has to be done by the purchasing agents who are left in the departments, and as the requisitions must be complied with literally, we are depriving the Purchasing Commission of practically the only usefulness that they could have. I am entirely new in public life, and I can only surmise how patronage has entered into govermental purchasing. I take it that the practice, if it ever existed, must have been that the manufacturer or dealer worked through the member, that the member worked through the minister and ' that favours were thus given to party friends.
But in this case the purchasing agents in the different departments, who come under the Civil Service Act that was passed by this House last session, are as free from political influence as will be the commissioners to be appointed under this Bill, for the simple reason that the purchasing agent in the department is not subject to the minister. His position is just as safe, so far as the influence of the minister is concerned, as would be the position of any member of the commission. Reverting to what I said a moment ago about the requisitions, the fact remains that if there has been patronage, the present Bill provides for a condition worse than that from which we are trying to get away. It will give to those in the department who will do the requisitioning an opportunity so to requisition goods that those goods will have to be supplied by the people whom the purchasing agent desires shall supply them, and there will be no departmental responsibility for their action, If the experience of the Government and of the departments has been that co-ordination is necessary in connection with certain purchasing, that coordination can be brought about without creating a department with such an elaborate staff as it is evidently the intention that this department shall have.

Prime Minister had better think over this matter. It is getting very late in the session, and there is determined opposition to this proposition. Is there any objection to having the resolution pass under the very reasonable conditions which I have

subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: I think there are two courses, and two only *fohich we ought to be asked to take. If we are to carry the resolution I see no reason for stopping this debate. It is possible to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition that we report progress. There is a great deal of force in his other request. This is very contentious legislation, opposed very strongly by a large number of members-if they take the attitude in the House that they take in conversation-on the Unionist side of the House. ,1 wish to endorse what the leader of the Opposition said about the able speech of my hon. friend from Lanark. I think it was a complete answer from a man of very large business experience-a man who has the power to form very clear views based on that experience, and the power of expressing those views very clearly. However, I do not wish to make a speech at this time of the morning, but I do not think the Committee should allow the resolution to pass. We had better go on with the debate.

subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
The minister has not answered the argument against the expense. The establishment of a new department is a serious matter. Any one who wishes ito satisfy himself on that score has only to look at the Estimates for the present year and see the enormous increase that has taken place in the expenditure on civil government. The expenditure has grown very rapidly indeed during the last three years, and the great increase is quite unjustifiable. Now it is proposed to add another department. It will be an expensive department, with experts and expensive men, if it is to be any good at all. The minister has not satisfied me, and I do not think he has satisfied the Committee why this very large expenditure should foe undertaken at the present (time. As to the cost of civil government, I find by the Public Accounts for the year 1911 the last year for which the late Government was responsible, civil government cost $4,774,678, and in the year 1918 $6,890,952.45, an increase of 50 per cent during the administration of my right hon. friend. The question is, what have we got for it? Are we better governed? Has this enormous increase brought greater efficiency in the departments that we had before? We are multiplying departments all the time, year after year. If I remember

rightly, at the time my right hon. friend came into power we had fourteen departments and fourteen ministers, and now we have twenty-one, I think. The increase in the number of ministers is 50 per cent, and the increase in the number of departments is enormous. Now it is proposed to create still another department, with a staff of expensive officials, typists, accountants, and so on. To my mind the principle is unsound. We now have purchasing agents in different departments-in the post office department, in the Department of Militia and Defence, in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and perhaps in some others. These purchasing agents are specialists for their own departments, but no man can be a specialist in everything. A man who is a specialist in buying post office supplies cannot be a specialist in buying supplies for the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I think we are better off with the specialists we have now; I think they will give us greater efficiency than we should have under this new organization. Hon. gentlemen would not propose such a centralization in other matters. We have engineers, for example, in the Department of Public Works, in the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and in the Department of Railways and Canals. Would my hon. friend think it would be a good thing to combine all the engineering departments of the Government? It would not. On the face of it it would be a bad move. I think the principle that all the purchasing of the Government can be successfully combined under one head is unsound. It would not produce the results my hon. friend expects.
Those are the two objections I have to the proposal-the enormous cost, and the fact that it relieves the minister of responsibility. It will involve the same old troubles that we have always had. mistakes in purchases, and graft. We will have irregularities and no one will be responsible, for the minister will be able to point to the commission that this House of Commons has organized, and to throw the whole blame on it, disclaiming any responsibility. I have also mentioned the question of expense, and this commission will not add to the efficiency of the public service. The minister has not shown us how it is going to put an end to the patronage abuses by the fact that it is one large concern instead of the smaller ones in the different departments. A few years ago the printing and advertising of the different departments was placed under one head in the office of the King's Printer.
That matter was investigated this year in the Public Accounts Committee, and we discovered that this officer was simply a figurehead, doing what some official in the departments told him. He received advertisements from the department for insertion in the papers, and he got a list of the papers in which he was to put them. He swore very positively that he had no patronage list, but when we asked him how he managed to distribute the advertisements among the various newspapers he told us that he received a list of newspapers in which to put the advertisement. We asked him if that was not a patronage list, and he said, no, it was not a patronage list. He gave it a new name; he called it a " selection." We took his " selection " and read it over, and in connection with my own province he was asked if he found on the list the Acadia Recorder, the Sydney Record, the Eastern Chronicle, the Lunen-bury Progress, in regard to each of which he said, no. I went over the names of all *the newspapers I knew of in my province that were Liberal, and none of them was on the list. I asked how it happened that the Liberal newspapers in Nova Scotia were omitted from his selection, and he said he did not know; he said " I cannot tell." That is the way myhon.friendhasabolished patronage, and nothing has been said in this discussion to convince a reasonable man that we will get rid of patronage by the establishing of this commission.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
I am not going into the statistics that have been alluded to by my hon. friend, but I am going to make this assertion, based on the experience of four years, that during that time there has not been, to my knowledge, the slightest attempt to exercise political patronage in respect of the work of the War Purchasing Commission. More than that, I firmly and sincerely believe that I am well within the bounds of moderation when I say that during the past four years that commission has saved to the people of the country more than would be expended in the maintenance of this proposed commission during the next fifty years. I have not the slightest doubt, speaking with most earnest conviction, that I am well within the bounds of moderation in this statement. I am perfectly desirous of giving every reasonable opportunity to discuss this measure. Hon. gentlemen have convictions upon it, and I hope that none of them will forget that I have some convictions on it also. It really does seem remarkable that when a Government is making a most earnest attempt, according

to the best light of which it is possessed, to rid itself and future governments of the evils of patronage, of which I have had some experience both while in opposition and while in office, the attempt should be met with such resistance on both sides of the House. I think that upon reflection we all shall be disposed to agree that the elimination of political patronage, whether in the appointment of public servants or in the purchase of public supplies, is eminently in the public interest. I am quite willing to be instructed if I can be instructed on the subject; but I do not know-and I have devoted a great deal of thought to the matter-of any other means by which that evil can be eliminated in this country than by some such action as is suggested in this Bill. If any hon. gentleman in this House, or any one out of the House, can suggest to me some better method in the public interest by which that very desirable consummation can be reached, I am perfectly ready to consider it; and, if after the best consideration we can give to such method it would seem to offer a better means 'than that provided in this Bill, I should be willing to accept it. It is as to the purpose and not the particular method provided by this Bill that I am in earnest, and more than that, in deadly earnest. The hour is rather late. I should have been glad if hon. gentlemen who are opposed to the Bill could have seen their way clear to continue the discussion upon the main resolution under what I thought was a very reasonable offer, namely, unlimited discussion upon that resolution. But under the circumstances I will not insist, and I therefore move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Motion agreed to and progress reported.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that a Message has been received from the Senate informing this House that the Senate doth concur in their message of the 27th June, ultimo, and also to the amendments made by the House of Commons to the Bill " A ", intituled: " An Act to consolidate and amend the Railway Act ", without any amendment.
On the motion of Sir Robert Borden the House adjourned at 12.35 a.m. (Thursday).
Thursday, July 3, 1919.
